arXiv:1805.08760v5 [math-ph] 11 Jan 2019

Moments of random matrices and
hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials

Fabio Deelan Cunden F. D. Cunden
School of Mathematics and Statistics, University College Dublin, Belfield, Dublin 4, Ireland , Francesco Mezzadri F. Mezzadri
School of Mathematics, University of Bristol, University Walk, Bristol BS8 1TW, United Kingdom , Neil O’Connell N. O’Connell
School of Mathematics and Statistics, University College Dublin, Belfield, Dublin 4, Ireland and Nick Simm N. Simm
Mathematics Department, University of Sussex, Brighton, BN1 9RH, United Kingdom
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We establish a new connection between moments of n×nn\times n random matrices XnX_{n} and hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials. Specifically, we consider moments 𝔼​Tr⁡Xn−s\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-s} as a function of the complex variable s∈ℂs\in\mathbb{C}, whose analytic structure we describe completely. We discover several remarkable features, including a reflection symmetry (or functional equation), zeros on a critical line in the complex plane, and orthogonality relations. An application of the theory resolves part of an integrality conjecture of Cunden et al. [F. D. Cunden, F. Mezzadri, N. J. Simm and P. Vivo, J. Math. Phys. 57 (2016)] on the time-delay matrix of chaotic cavities. In each of the classical ensembles of random matrix theory (Gaussian, Laguerre, Jacobi) we characterise the moments in terms of the Askey scheme of hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials. We also calculate the leading order n→∞n\to\infty asymptotics of the moments and discuss their symmetries and zeroes. We discuss aspects of these phenomena beyond the random matrix setting, including the Mellin transform of products and Wronskians of pairs of classical orthogonal polynomials. When the random matrix model has orthogonal or symplectic symmetry, we obtain a new duality formula relating their moments to hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials.

1. Introduction

In this paper we present a novel approach to the moments of the classical ensembles of random matrices. Much of random matrix theory is devoted to moments 𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k} (k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}) of random matrices of finite or asymptotically large size nn. The Gaussian, Laguerre and Jacobi unitary ensembles have been extensively studied and virtually everything is known about the moments as functions of the matrix size nn. In particular, for the GUE, 𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k} is a polynomial in nn. This fact is a consequence of Wick’s theorem, it is usually called ‘genus expansion’, and it is at the heart of several successful theories such as the topological recursion [6, 33]. For example, the 44-th moment of GUE matrices of size nn is

1n​𝔼​Tr⁡Xn8=14​n4+70​n2+21.\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{8}=14n^{4}+70n^{2}+21.

In contrast to the wealth of results on moments as functions of the size nn, less attention has been devoted to them as functions of the order kk. One of the consequences is that some remarkable properties have been somehow missed. The theory described in this paper is intended to fill this gap. By looking at the moments as functions of kk, we gain access to additional structure. Several results contained in this paper are in fact facets of the same phenomenon, which appears to be a new observation: moments 𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k} of classical matrix ensembles, if properly normalized, are hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials as functions of kk. For example, for a GUE random matrix of size n=4n=4

1(2​k−1)!!​𝔼​Tr⁡X42​k=43​k3+4​k2+203​k+4,\frac{1}{(2k-1)!!}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{4}^{2k}=\frac{4}{3}k^{3}+4k^{2}+\frac{20}{3}k+4,

and this polynomial is actually a Meixner polynomial. In fact, the moments are essentially Meixner polynomials as functions of (n−1)(n-1), too.

During our investigation it became natural to consider complex moments 𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k} (k∈ℂk\in\mathbb{C}) or, equivalently, averages of spectral zeta functions of random matrices.

1.1. Spectral zeta functions of random matrices

There exist various generalizations of the Riemann ζ\zeta-function, associated with operator spectra and which are generically called spectral zeta functions.

Consider a compact operator AA on a separable Hilbert space. Then A​A∗AA^{*} is a nonnegative operator, so that |A|=A​A∗|A|=AA^{*} makes sense. The singular values of AA are defined as the (nonzero) eigenvalues of |A||A|. If AA is self-adjoint with discrete spectrum λ1,λ2,…\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\dots, the singular values are |λ1|,|λ2|,…|\lambda_{1}|,|\lambda_{2}|,\dots. The Dirichlet series representation of the Riemann zeta function ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) suggests to define the spectral zeta function ζA​(s)\zeta_{A}(s) of the operator AA as the maximal analytic continuation of the series

∑j≥1|λj|−s\sum_{j\geq 1}|\lambda_{j}|^{-s}

(this is also called Minakshisundaram–Pleijel [63] zeta function of AA.) In this sense, the Riemann ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) is the spectral zeta of the integer spectrum λj=j\lambda_{j}=j. Several authors have posed the question of how the ‘spectral’ properties of Riemann’s zeta function carry over (or not) to various spectral zeta functions [74]; classical properties of the Riemann zeta function are:

  1. (1)

    Functional equation: the function ξ(s)=π−s/2Γ(s/2)ζ(s)\xi(s)=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s) satisfies ξ⁡(1−s)=ξ⁡(s)\xi(1-s)=\xi(s);

  2. (2)

    Meromorphic structure: ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) is analytic in ℂ∖{1}\mathbb{C}\setminus\{1\};

  3. (3)

    Special values: trivial zeros ζ⁡(−2​j)=0\zeta(-2j)=0 for j=1,2,…j=1,2,\dots;

  4. (4)

    Complex zeros of ζ⁡(s)\zeta(s) and the Riemann hypothesis (RH): the complex Riemann zeros are in the critical strip 0<Re⁡(s)<10<\operatorname{Re}(s)<1 and enjoy the reflection symmetries along the real axis and the line Re⁡(s)=1/2\operatorname{Re}(s)=1/2. It is conjectured (RH) that the nontrivial zeros all lie on the critical line Re⁡(s)=1/2\operatorname{Re}(s)=1/2.

Let XnX_{n} be a n×nn\small\times n random Hermitian matrix, and denote by λ1,…,λn\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n} its eigenvalues. Assume that, with full probability, 00 is not in the spectrum of XnX_{n} (this is certainly true for the classical ensembles of random matrices). We proceed to define the averaged spectral zeta function ζXn​(s)\zeta_{X_{n}}(s) as the maximal analytic continuation of

𝔼​ζXn​(s)=𝔼​Tr⁡|Xn|−s=𝔼​∑j=1n|λj|−s.\mathbb{E}\,\zeta_{X_{n}}(s)=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}|X_{n}|^{-s}=\mathbb{E}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|\lambda_{j}|^{-s}.

Note that 𝔼​ζXn​(s)\mathbb{E}\,\zeta_{X_{n}}(s) is not a random function. Much of the paper is devoted to pointing out the analytic structure of 𝔼​ζXn​(s)\mathbb{E}\,\zeta_{X_{n}}(s) when XnX_{n} comes from the Gaussian, Laguerre or Jacobi ensembles.

1.2. Time-delay matrix of chaotic cavities

Random matrix theory provides a mathematical framework to develop a statistical theory of quantum transport. This theory is believed to apply in particular to mesoscopic conductors confined in space, often referred as quantum dots, connected to the environment through ideal leads. For these systems, Brouwer, Frahm and Beenakker [18], showed that the proper delay times are distributed as the inverse of the eigenvalues of matrices XnX_{n} in the Laguerre ensemble (the size nn being the number of scattering channels) with Dyson index β∈{1,2,4}\beta\in\{1,2,4\} labelling the classical symmetry classes, and parameter α=n\alpha=n.

The moments of the proper delay times have been studied using both random matrix theory [25, 27, 28, 43, 56, 62, 70, 71] and semiclassical scattering orbit theory [68, 14, 50]. Of course, the subject of moments on rather general matrix ensembles has been extensively studied. There is, however, one important complication here: the moments of the time-delay matrix are singular spectral linear statistic on the Laguerre ensemble. (Invariant random matrix ensembles with singular potentials received considerable interest in recent years in mathematical physics, see, e.g. Refs. [4, 10, 15, 22, 60, 17].)

In [25, 27, 28], it was conjectured that the 1/n1/n-expansion of the cumulants of power traces for the time-delay matrix of quantum dots has positive integer coefficients. In this paper we prove that the conjecture is true for the first order cumulants, i.e. the moments, when β=2\beta=2 (systems without broken time reversal symmetry).

1.3. Mellin transform of orthogonal polynomials

The averaged zeta function is related to the Mellin transform of the one-point correlation function11 1 See Section 3 for the definition of the one-point function and the important identity (3.4).. In the classical unitary invariant ensembles, by using the well-known determinantal formulae and Christoffel-Darboux formula, the one-point correlation function can be written as a Wronskian

ρn(2)​(x)=∑j=0n−1ψj2​(x)=kn−1kn​Wr⁡(ψn−1​(x),ψn​(x)),\rho^{(2)}_{n}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\psi_{j}^{2}(x)=\frac{k_{n-1}}{k_{n}}\operatorname{Wr}(\psi_{n-1}(x),\psi_{n}(x)),

where ψj​(x)\psi_{j}(x) are the normalized Hermite, Laguerre or Jacobi wavefunctions with leading coefficient kjk_{j}. (The superscript stands for β=2\beta=2.) The Mellin transform of a function f⁡(x)f(x) is defined by the integral

ℳ⁡[f⁡(x);s]=∫0∞f⁡(x)​xs−1​𝑑x,\mathcal{M}\left[f(x);s\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty}f(x)x^{s-1}dx,

when it exists. We set f∗​(s)=ℳ⁡[f⁡(x);s]f^{*}(s)=\mathcal{M}\left[f(x);s\right]. Of course, 𝔼​ζXn​(s)=ρn(2),∗​(1−s)\mathbb{E}\,\zeta_{X_{n}}(s)=\rho^{(2),*}_{n}(1-s). In all instances in this paper, the Mellin transforms have meromorphic extensions to all of ℂ\mathbb{C} with simple poles (see Appendix B.1).

Bump and Ng [20] and Bump, Choi, Kurlberg and Vaaler [21] made the remarkable observation that the Mellin transforms of Hermite and Laguerre functions ψj​(x)\psi_{j}(x) form families of orthogonal polynomials (OP’s) and have zeros on the critical line Re⁡(s)=1/2\operatorname{Re}(s)=1/2. (Jacobi functions were not considered by them.) A few years later, Coffey [23] and Coffey and Lettington [24] pointed out that the polynomials described by Bump et al. were hypergeometric OP’s and investigated other families.

Indeed, we show that for the classical matrix ensembles, the Mellin transform ρn(2),∗​(s)\rho^{(2),*}_{n}(s) of a Wronskian of two adjacent wavefunctions is a hypergeometric OP (up to a factor containing ratios of Gamma functions). We stress that the proof does not go along the lines of the method of Bump et al.. They started from the orthogonality of the classical wavefunctions which is preserved by the Mellin transform (a unitary operator in L2L^{2}). In our case, by explicit computations, we identify a discrete Sturm-Liouville (S-L) problem satisfied by ρn(2),∗​(s)\rho^{(2),*}_{n}(s) (as a function of ss) and this turns out to be the same S-L of the classical hypergeometric OP’s. We remark that the Mellin transforms ρn(2),∗​(s)\rho^{(2),*}_{n}(s) of ρn(2)​(x)\rho^{(2)}_{n}(x) do have a probabilistic meaning (moments of random matrices). The Mellin transforms ψj∗​(s)\psi_{j}^{*}(s) studied in [20, 21], while not unmotivated, do not have an obvious probabilistic interpretation.

Once the analytic structure of the Mellin transform of Wr⁡(ψn​(x),ψn+1​(x))\operatorname{Wr}(\psi_{n}(x),\psi_{n+1}(x)) was established, it became natural for us to look for similar polynomial properties for Wronskians of nonadjacent wavefunctions Wr⁡(ψn​(x),ψn+k​(x))\operatorname{Wr}(\psi_{n}(x),\psi_{n+k}(x)), k>1k>1. Such Wronskians do not have a random matrix interpretation. Nevertheless, they have a certain interest in mathematical physics as they appear when applying Darboux-Crum [29] transformations on a Schrödinger operator to generate families of exceptional orthogonal polynomials [39, 49, 69, 41].

1.4. Orthogonal and symplectic ensembles

The theory developed for the classical ensembles of complex random matrices suggested to look for similar polynomial properties in the real and quaternionic cases (orthogonal and symplectic ensembles).

Now a fundamental insight came from recursion formulae satisfied by orthogonal / symplectic moments coupled with moments of the corresponding unitary ensembles (see [53] in the Gaussian case and [28] in the Laguerre ensemble). It turns out that for the classical ensembles of random matrices with orthogonal and symplectic symmetries, certain combinations of moments satisfy three term recursion formulae which, again, correspond to the S-L equations defining families of hypergeometric OP’s. Therefore, this combination of moments plays the role of the single moments in the unitary case: they satisfy three term recursions, have hypergeometric OP factors, reflection symmetries, zeros on a vertical line, etc.

The (single) moments of the symplectic ensembles do have polynomial factors, but these do not belong to the Askey scheme. In the orthogonal cases, we use a novel duality formula (based on the results by Adler et al. [3]) to write the moments of real random matrices of odd dimension as quaternionic moments plus a remainder containing an orthogonal polynomial factor.

Coupling this result with a classical duality between orthogonal and symplectic ensembles, we discover a functional equation for moments of real random matrices.

1.5. Outline

The paper has the following structure:

  • •

    In Section 2 the physics motivations and application to quantum transport in chaotic cavities are presented;

  • •

    In Section 3 we set some notation and we recall the definition of the classical ensembles of random matrices and hypergeometric OP’s;

  • •

    In Section 4 we present the main results along with their proofs for the Gaussian, Laguerre and Jacobi unitary ensembles;

  • •

    In Section 5 we discuss the large-nn asymptotics of the spectral zeta functions;

  • •

    In Section 6 we discuss the relation of our findings with earlier works on the Mellin transform of classical orthogonal polynomials; then, we extend our results beyond random matrix theory by considering Mellin transforms of products and Wronskians of generic pairs of orthogonal polynomials;

  • •

    In Section 7 we discuss the extension of duality formulae between moments of random matrices to higher order cumulants;

  • •

    In Section 8 we consider the classical orthogonal and symplectic ensembles and, in particular, present a new duality formula relating their moments to hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials.

2. Motivation and applications

One of the original motivations for this work was to make some progress on an integrality conjecture for the 1/n1/n-expansion of the Laguerre ensemble put forward in [25, 27, 28]. The problem originated from a random matrix approach to quantum transport in chaotic cavities.

In this section, we will first present some of our findings on the Laguerre ensemble. Then we will briefly review the connection between the Laguerre ensemble and the time-delay matrix in chaotic cavities, and explain the applicability of our results to the integrality conjecture.

2.1. The Laguerre ensemble: reciprocity law and spectral zeta function

Let XnX_{n} be a random matrix from the Laguerre Unitary Ensemble (LUE) with parameter m≥nm\geq n. That is, XnX_{n} is distributed according to

(2.1) d​ℙ​(X)=1Z​(detXα)​exp⁡(−Tr⁡X)​d​Xd\mathbb{P}(X)=\frac{1}{Z}(\det X^{\alpha})\exp(-\operatorname{Tr}X)dX

on the space 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} of nonnegative Hermitian matrices, where d​XdX is Lebesgue measure on 𝒫n≃ℝn2\mathcal{P}_{n}\simeq\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}}, ZZ the normalizing constant, and α=m−n\alpha=m-n.

Consider for integer k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, the (inverse) moments

(2.2) 𝔼​Tr⁡Xn−k=𝔼​∑j=1nλj−k,\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k}=\mathbb{E}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{j}^{-k},

where λ1,…,λn\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n} are the eigenvalues of XnX_{n}. The above moments are finite if and only if k≤αk\leq\alpha [51]. We will prove the following remarkable property of these moments.

Proposition 2.1 (Reciprocity law for LUE).
(2.3) 𝔼​Tr⁡Xn−(k+1)=(∏j=−kk1α+j)​𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk.\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-(k+1)}=\left(\prod_{j=-k}^{k}\frac{1}{\alpha+j}\right)\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k}.

The above identity can be verified using the recurrence relation for moments proved by Haagerup and Thorbjørnsen [44] and extended to inverse moments in [28]. This gives an explicit formula for the inverse moments given known identities for positive moments. For instance,

𝔼​Tr⁡Xn0\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{0} =n\displaystyle=n 𝔼​Tr⁡Xn−1\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-1} =nα\displaystyle=\frac{n}{\alpha}
𝔼​Tr⁡Xn1\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{1} =n2+α​n\displaystyle=n^{2}+\alpha n 𝔼​Tr⁡Xn−2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-2} =n2+α​n(α−1)​α​(α+1)\displaystyle=\frac{n^{2}+\alpha n}{(\alpha-1)\alpha(\alpha+1)}
𝔼​Tr⁡Xn2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{2} =2​n3+3​α​n2+α2​n\displaystyle=2n^{3}+3\alpha n^{2}+\alpha^{2}n 𝔼​Tr⁡Xn−3\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-3} =2​n3+3​α​n2+α2​n(α−2)​(α−1)​α​(α+1)​(α+2).\displaystyle=\frac{2n^{3}+3\alpha n^{2}+\alpha^{2}n}{(\alpha-2)(\alpha-1)\alpha(\alpha+1)(\alpha+2)}.

It is natural to consider complex moments or, equivalently, the averaged LUE spectral zeta function defined as

(2.4) 𝔼​ζXn​(s)=𝔼​Tr⁡Xn−s=𝔼​∑jλj−s,for Re⁡(s)≤α,\mathbb{E}\zeta_{X_{n}}(s)=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-s}=\mathbb{E}\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}^{-s},\quad\text{for $\operatorname{Re}(s)\leq\alpha$},

and by analytic continuation for other values of ss. We list below a few remarkable properties of the averaged LUE spectral zeta function.

  1. (1)

    Functional equation: the reciprocity law (2.3) suggests to consider the function

    (2.5) ξn​(s)=1Γ⁡(1+α−s)​𝔼​ζXn​(s),\xi_{n}(s)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(1+\alpha-s)}\mathbb{E}\,\zeta_{X_{n}}(s),

    so that (2.3) becomes the functional equation

    (2.6) ξn​(1−s)=ξn​(s).\xi_{n}(1-s)=\xi_{n}(s).
  2. (2)

    Analytic structure: it turns out that 𝔼​ζXn​(s)\mathbb{E}\,\zeta_{X_{n}}(s) can be analytically extended to the whole complex plane; In particular, ξn​(s)\xi_{n}(s) is a polynomial of degree 2​(n−1)2(n-1).

  3. (3)

    Special values: trivial zeros 𝔼​ζXn​(1+α+j)=0\mathbb{E}\,\zeta_{X_{n}}(1+\alpha+j)=0 for j=1,2,…j=1,2,\dots;

  4. (4)

    Complex zeros and Riemann hypothesis: as for the Riemann zeta function, the set of complex zeros is symmetric with respect to reflections along the real axis and the critical line Re⁡(s)=1/2\operatorname{Re}(s)=1/2. It is tempting to ask whether a RH holds true for the averaged LUE zeta function. Amusingly, the answer is ‘Yes’: the nontrivial zeros of 𝔼​ζXn​(s)\mathbb{E}\,\zeta_{X_{n}}(s) all lie on the critical line Re⁡(s)=1/2\operatorname{Re}(s)=1/2.

These facts are an immediate consequences of the main results presented in Section 4. See Fig. 1 for a plot of the averaged LUE zeta function and Fig. 2 for an illustration of the zeros.

Remark.

For any fixed nn, the function ζXn​(s)\zeta_{X_{n}}(s) is a finite sum of exponentials. Therefore, without taking the average, ζXn​(s)\zeta_{X_{n}}(s) is a random analytic function in ℂ\mathbb{C} and never vanishes.

2.2. Application to quantum transport in chaotic cavities

In [25, 27], it was proposed that, for β∈{1,2}\beta\in\{1,2\}, the cumulants of the time-delay matrix of a ballistic chaotic cavity have a 1/n1/n-expansion with positive integer coefficients (similar to the genus expansion of Gaussian matrices). The precise conjectural statement is as follows.

Consider the measure (2.1) with α=n\alpha=n, and the rescaled inverse power traces

τk​(n)=nk−1​Tr⁡Xn−k(k≥0).\tau_{k}(n)=n^{k-1}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k}\quad(k\geq 0).

It is known that the expectation of τk​(n)\tau_{k}(n) has a 1/n1/n-expansion

𝔼​τk​(n)=∑g=0∞κg​(k)​n−g.\mathbb{E}\tau_{k}(n)=\sum_{g=0}^{\infty}\kappa_{g}(k)n^{-g}.
Conjecture ([28]).

κg​(k)∈ℕ\kappa_{g}(k)\in\mathbb{N}.

The conjecture was supported by a systematic computation of certain generating functions, and it is in agreement with the diagrammatic expansions of scattering orbit theory. The integrality of the coefficients in the large-nn expansion has been also conjectured in the real case (LOE) [28], and for higher order cumulants [25, 27].

The results reported in this paper resolve the conjecture in the complex case.

Theorem 2.2.

The above conjecture is true.

Proof.

To prove the Theorem we take advantage of the reciprocity law to use known results for positive moments of the Laguerre ensemble.

Let XnX_{n} be in the LUE with parameter α=m−n\alpha=m-n. For k≥0k\geq 0, from [45, Corollary 2.4] (see also [64, Exercise 12]) we read the formula

(2.7) 1nk+1​𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk=∑σ∈Skn#⁡(σ)+#⁡(γk​σ−1)−(k+1)​(mn)#⁡(σ),\frac{1}{n^{k+1}}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k}=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{k}}n^{\#(\sigma)+\#(\gamma_{k}\sigma^{-1})-(k+1)}\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)^{\#(\sigma)},

where SkS_{k} is the symmetric group, and for a permutation σ∈Sk\sigma\in S_{k}, #⁡(σ)\#(\sigma) denotes the number of cycles in σ\sigma. By γk\gamma_{k} we denote the kk-cycle (1 2 3​…​k)(1\;2\;3\;\ldots\;k). If m=c​nm=cn with c>0c>0, the above formula shows that 1nk+1​𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk\frac{1}{n^{k+1}}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k} is a polynomial in n−2n^{-2} with positive coefficients (see Lemma 4.5 below).

By the reciprocity law (2.3) with α=n\alpha=n (or, equivalently, c=2c=2)

(2.8) 𝔼​τk+1​(n)=(∏j=1k11−j2n2)​1nk+1​𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk.\mathbb{E}\tau_{k+1}(n)=\left(\prod_{j=1}^{k}\frac{1}{1-\frac{j^{2}}{n^{2}}}\right)\frac{1}{n^{k+1}}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k}.

The factor ∏j=1k(1−j2n2)−1\prod_{j=1}^{k}\left(1-\frac{j^{2}}{n^{2}}\right)^{-1} in (2.8) is a product of geometric series. Therefore, we have

(2.9) 𝔼​τk+1​(n)=∑σ∈Sk∑i1,…,ik=0∞(2#⁡(σ)​∏j=1kj2​ij)​n#⁡(σ)+#⁡(γk​σ−1)−(k+1)−2​(i1+⋯+ik),\mathbb{E}\tau_{k+1}(n)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{k}}\sum_{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}=0}^{\infty}\left(2^{\#(\sigma)}\prod_{j=1}^{k}j^{2i_{j}}\right)n^{\#(\sigma)+\#(\gamma_{k}\sigma^{-1})-(k+1)-2(i_{1}+\cdots+i_{k})},

and this readily prove that 𝔼​τk\mathbb{E}\tau_{k} has an expansion in n−2n^{-2} with positive integer coefficients. ∎

Remark.

From (2.7) we see that, if c∈ℕc\in\mathbb{N}, then 1nk+1​𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk\frac{1}{n^{k+1}}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k} (k≥0k\geq 0 integer) has a 1/n1/n-expansion with positive integer coefficients. The computation above shows that the integrality of the coefficients for the LUE negative moments also holds whenever c/(c−1)∈ℕc/(c-1)\in\mathbb{N}. Therefore, c=2c=2 is the only case when all moments 1nk+1​𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk\frac{1}{n^{k+1}}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k} (k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}) have integer coefficients in their large-nn expansion.

3. Notation and definitions

3.1. Classical ensembles of random matrices

We will consider expectations with respect to the measures

(3.1) 1Cn,β​∏j=1nwβ​(xj)​χI​(xj)​∏1≤j<k≤n|xk−xj|β​d​x1​⋯​d​xn\frac{1}{C_{n,\beta}}\prod_{j=1}^{n}w_{\beta}(x_{j})\chi_{I}(x_{j})\prod_{1\leq j<k\leq n}|x_{k}-x_{j}|^{\beta}dx_{1}\dotsm dx_{n}

for finite nn and for any value of β∈{1,2,4}\beta\in\{1,2,4\}. The value of β\beta corresponds to ensembles of real symmetric (β=1\beta=1), complex hermitian (β=2\beta=2) or quaternion self-dual matrices (β=4\beta=4). The function wβ​(x)w_{\beta}(x) is the weight of the ensemble:

(3.2) wβ​(x)={e−(β/2)x2/2,I=ℝ,x(β/2)​(m−n+1)−1​e−(β/2)​x,I=ℝ+,(1−x)(β/2)​(m1−n+1)−1​x(β/2)​(m2−n+1)−1,I=[0,1],w_{\beta}(x)=\begin{cases}e^{-(\beta/2)x^{2}/2},&I=\mathbb{R},\\ x^{(\beta/2)(m-n+1)-1}\;e^{-(\beta/2)x},&I=\mathbb{R}_{+},\\ (1-x)^{(\beta/2)(m_{1}-n+1)-1}\;x^{(\beta/2)(m_{2}-n+1)-1},&I=[0,1],\end{cases}

for Gaussian, Laguerre, and Jacobi, respectively. Cn,βC_{n,\beta} is a normalization constant which depends on the ensemble and is known explicitly [36]. For convenience we set α=m−n>0\alpha=m-n>0 in the Laguerre ensemble and α1=m1−n>0,α2=m2−n>0\alpha_{1}=m_{1}-n>0,\;\alpha_{2}=m_{2}-n>0 in the Jacobi ensemble.

We define the one-point eigenvalue density ρn(β)​(x)\rho^{(\beta)}_{n}(x) corresponding to (3.1) by

(3.3) ρn(β)​(x)=𝔼⁡(∑j=1nδ⁡(x−xj))\rho^{(\beta)}_{n}(x)=\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\delta(x-x_{j})\right)

We will call (3.3) the eigenvalue density corresponding to the weight wβ​(x)w_{\beta}(x) defining the expectation over (3.1). The following identity easily follows from the definitions (3.3) and (3.1):

(3.4) 𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk=∫Ixk​ρn(β)​(x)​𝑑x.\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k}=\int_{I}\,x^{k}\rho^{(\beta)}_{n}(x)\,dx.

3.2. Hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials

We use the standard notation for hypergeometric functions

Fqp​(a1,…,apb1,…,bq,z)=∑j=0∞(a1)j⋯(ap)j(b1)j⋯(bq)j​zjj!,{}_{p}F_{q}\left(\begin{matrix}a_{1},\dots,a_{p}\\ b_{1},\dots,b_{q}\end{matrix};z\right)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a_{1})_{j}\cdots(a_{p})_{j}}{(b_{1})_{j}\cdots(b_{q})_{j}}\frac{z^{j}}{j!},

where (q)n=Γ⁡(q+n)/Γ⁡(q)(q)_{n}=\Gamma(q+n)/\Gamma(q). We need to introduce some families of hypergeometric OP’s [48]. Recall that there are three types of hypergeometric OP’s:

  1. (1)

    Polynomials of the first type are solutions of usual S-L problems for second order differential operators: Jacobi Pn(α1,α2)​(x)P^{(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})}_{n}(x) and its degenerations, Laguerre Ln(α)​(x)L^{(\alpha)}_{n}(x) and Hermite Hn​(x)H_{n}(x). They have a hypergeometric representation, but they are perhaps better known by the Rodrigues-type formulae

    (3.5) Hn​(x)\displaystyle H_{n}(x) =(−1)n​ex2​dnd​xn​e−x2,\displaystyle=(-1)^{n}\,e^{x^{2}}\frac{d^{n}}{dx^{n}}e^{-x^{2}},
    (3.6) Ln(α)​(x)\displaystyle L_{n}^{(\alpha)}(x) =1n!​x−α​ex​dnd​xn​xn+α​e−x,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n!}\,x^{-\alpha}e^{x}\frac{d^{n}}{dx^{n}}x^{n+\alpha}e^{-x},
    (3.7) Pn(α1,α2)​(x)\displaystyle P_{n}^{(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})}(x) =1n!​(−1)n(1−x)α1​xα2​dnd​xn​(1−x)α1+n​xα2+n.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n!}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{(1-x)^{\alpha_{1}}x^{\alpha_{2}}}\frac{d^{n}}{dx^{n}}(1-x)^{\alpha_{1}+n}x^{\alpha_{2}+n}.

    Note that the Jacobi polynomials considered in this paper are orthogonal with respect to the measure (1−x)α1​xα2​d​x(1-x)^{\alpha_{1}}x^{\alpha_{2}}dx on the unit interval [0,1][0,1];

  2. (2)

    Polynomials of the second type are solutions of discrete S-L problems (three-terms recurrence relations) with real coefficients: Racah Rn​(λ⁡(x),α,β,γ,δ)R_{n}(\lambda(x);\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta), including its degenerations Hahn Qn​(x,α,β,N)Q_{n}(x;\alpha,\beta,N), dual Hahn Rn​(λ⁡(x),γ,δ,N)R_{n}(\lambda(x);\gamma,\delta,N), Meixner Mn​(x,β,c)M_{n}(x;\beta,c), etc. They can be represented as finite hypergeometric series

    (3.8) Rn​(λ⁡(x),α,β,γ,δ)\displaystyle R_{n}(\lambda(x);\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta) =F34​(−n,n+α+β+1,−x,x+γ+δ+1α+1,β+δ+1,γ+1,1)\displaystyle=\;{}_{4}F_{3}\left(\begin{matrix}-n,n+\alpha+\beta+1,-x,x+\gamma+\delta+1\\ \alpha+1,\beta+\delta+1,\gamma+1\end{matrix};1\right)
    (3.9) Qn​(x,α,β,N)\displaystyle Q_{n}(x;\alpha,\beta,N) =F23​(−n,n+α+β+1,−xα+1,−N,1)\displaystyle={}_{3}F_{2}\left(\begin{matrix}-n,n+\alpha+\beta+1,-x\\ \alpha+1,-N\end{matrix};1\right)
    (3.10) Rn​(λ⁡(x),γ,δ,N)\displaystyle R_{n}(\lambda(x);\gamma,\delta,N) =F23​(−n,−x,x+γ+δ+1γ+1,−N,1)\displaystyle={}_{3}F_{2}\left(\begin{matrix}-n,-x,x+\gamma+\delta+1\\ \gamma+1,-N\end{matrix};1\right)
    (3.11) Mn​(x,β,c)\displaystyle M_{n}(x;\beta,c) =F12​(−n,−xβ,1−1c),\displaystyle={}_{2}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}-n,-x\\ \beta\end{matrix};1-\frac{1}{c}\right),

    where λ⁡(x)=x⁡(x+γ+δ+1)\lambda(x)=x(x+\gamma+\delta+1). Note that some authors define the Meixner polynomials as mn​(x,β,c)=(β)n​Mn​(x,β,c)m_{n}(x;\beta,c)=(\beta)_{n}M_{n}(x;\beta,c);

  3. (3)

    Polynomials of the third type are solutions of discrete S-L problems with complex coefficients: Wilson Wn​(x2,a,b,c,d)W_{n}(x^{2};a,b,c,d) including its degenerations, continuous dual Hahn Sn​(x2,a,b,c)S_{n}(x^{2};\;a,b,c), continuous Hahn pn​(x,a,b,c,d)p_{n}(x;a,b,c,d), Meixner-Pollaczek Pn(λ)​(x,ϕ)P_{n}^{(\lambda)}(x;\phi), etc. They have the following hypergeometric representations:

    Wn​(x2,a,b,c,d)\displaystyle W_{n}(x^{2};a,b,c,d) =(a+b)n​(a+c)n​(a+d)n\displaystyle=(a+b)_{n}(a+c)_{n}(a+d)_{n}
    (3.12) ×F34​(−n,n+a+b+c+d−1,a+i​x,a−i​xa+b,a+c,a+d,1)\displaystyle\small\times\;{}_{4}F_{3}\left(\begin{matrix}-n,n+a+b+c+d-1,a+ix,a-ix\\ a+b,a+c,a+d\end{matrix};1\right)
    (3.13) Sn​(x2,a,b,c)\displaystyle S_{n}(x^{2};a,b,c) =(a+b)n​(a+c)n​F23​(−n,a+i​x,a−i​xa+b,a+c,1)\displaystyle=(a+b)_{n}(a+c)_{n}\;{}_{3}F_{2}\left(\begin{matrix}-n,a+ix,a-ix\\ a+b,a+c\end{matrix};1\right)
    pn​(x,a,b,c,d)\displaystyle p_{n}(x;a,b,c,d) =inn!​(a+c)n​(a+d)n\displaystyle=\frac{i^{n}}{n!}(a+c)_{n}(a+d)_{n}
    (3.14) ×F23​(−n,n+a+b+c+d−1,a+i​xa+c,a+d,1)\displaystyle\small\times{}_{3}F_{2}\left(\begin{matrix}-n,n+a+b+c+d-1,a+ix\\ a+c,a+d\end{matrix};1\right)
    (3.15) Pn(λ)​(x,ϕ)\displaystyle P_{n}^{(\lambda)}(x;\phi) =(2​λ)n​ei​n​ϕn!​F12​(−n,λ+i​x2​λ,1−e2​i​ϕ).\displaystyle=(2\lambda)_{n}\frac{e^{in\phi}}{n!}{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}-n,\lambda+ix\\ 2\lambda\end{matrix};1-e^{2i\phi}\right).

At the top of the hierarchy of hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials are the Wilson and Racah polynomials. In this paper, the parameter ranges are such that it is most natural to consider the polynomials which appear as Wilson polynomials and their degenerations, specifically continuous dual Hahn and Meixner-Pollaczek polynomials. The reader can find the common notation and the most important properties of hypergeometric OP’s in [48, Section 9].

4. Unitary ensembles

It is known that the kk-th moments of the classical unitary invariant ensembles of random matrices XnX_{n} of dimension nn are polynomials in nn (or in 1/n1/n after rescaling). Here we show that the (completed) moments can also be seen as polynomials in the parameter kk. These polynomials are hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials OP’s belonging to the Askey scheme [8]. The polynomial property suggests to consider complex moments or, equivalently, averages of spectral zeta functions. For the three classical ensembles, define

ζXn​(s)=Tr⁡|Xn|−s,Xn∼{GUE,LUE,JUE},\zeta_{X_{n}}(s)=\operatorname{Tr}|X_{n}|^{-s},\quad X_{n}\sim\{\mathrm{GUE},\mathrm{LUE},\mathrm{JUE}\},

and

ξn​(s)={22​sΓ⁡(1/2−2​s)​𝔼​ζXn​(4​s)if Xn∼GUE,1Γ⁡(1+α−s)​𝔼​ζXn​(s)if Xn∼LUE,Γ⁡(1+α1+α2+2​n−s)Γ⁡(1+α2−s)​𝔼​(ζXn​(s)−ζXn​(s−1))if Xn∼JUE,\xi_{n}(s)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l@{\quad}cr}\displaystyle\frac{2^{2s}}{\Gamma\left(1/2-2s\right)}\;\mathbb{E}\,\zeta_{X_{n}}(4s)&&\text{if $X_{n}\sim\mathrm{GUE}$}\ ,\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\Gamma(1+\alpha-s)}\;\mathbb{E}\,\zeta_{X_{n}}(s)&&\text{if $X_{n}\sim\mathrm{LUE}$}\ ,\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\Gamma(1+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n-s)}{\Gamma(1+\alpha_{2}-s)}\;\mathbb{E}\left(\zeta_{X_{n}}(s)-\zeta_{X_{n}}(s-1)\right)&&\text{if $X_{n}\sim\mathrm{JUE}$}\ ,\end{array}\right.

when the expectations exist (s<1/4s<1/4, s<α+1s<\alpha+1, and s<α2+1s<\alpha_{2}+1 for GUE\mathrm{GUE}, LUE\mathrm{LUE}, and JUE\mathrm{JUE}, respectively) and by analytic continuation otherwise (see Appendix B.1).

We can now state the first result.

Theorem 4.1.

For all nn, ξn​(s)\xi_{n}(s) is a hypergeometric orthogonal polynomial:

ξn​(s)={i1−nπ​Pn−1(1)​(2​x,π/2)if Xn∼GUE1Γ⁡(n)​Γ​(α+n)​Sn−1​(x2,32,12,α+12)if Xn∼LUEΓ⁡(α1+α2+n+1)Γ⁡(n)​Γ​(α2+n)​(−1)n−1​(α1+n)×Wn−1​(x2,32,12,α2+12,12−α1−α2−2​n)if Xn∼JUE,\xi_{n}(s)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l@{\quad}cr}\displaystyle\frac{i^{1-n}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\;P^{(1)}_{n-1}\left(2x;\;\pi/2\right)&\text{if $X_{n}\sim\mathrm{GUE}$}\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\Gamma(n)\Gamma(\alpha+n)}\;S_{n-1}\left(x^{2};\;\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2},\alpha+\frac{1}{2}\right)&\text{if $X_{n}\sim\mathrm{LUE}$}\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+n+1)}{\Gamma(n)\Gamma(\alpha_{2}+n)}(-1)^{n-1}(\alpha_{1}+n)\\ \small\times\;\displaystyle W_{n-1}\left(x^{2};\;\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2},\alpha_{2}+\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}-2n\right)\hfil\hskip 9.24994pt&\text{if $X_{n}\sim\mathrm{JUE}$}\ ,\end{array}\right.

where x=i⁡(1/2−s)x=i(1/2-s). In particular, ξn​(s)\xi_{n}(s) satisfies the functional equation ξn​(s)=ξn​(1−s)\xi_{n}(s)=\xi_{n}(1-s) in the LUE and JUE cases, and ξn​(s)=(−1)n−1​ξn​(1−s)\xi_{n}(s)=(-1)^{n-1}\xi_{n}(1-s) for the GUE. Moreover, all its zeros lie on the critical line Re⁡(s)=1/2\operatorname{Re}(s)=1/2.

Proof.

See Theorems 4.2, 4.4 and 4.7 below. ∎

The weights of the OP’s in Theorem 4.1 are

w⁡(s)={|2​π​Γ​(2​s)|2if Xn∼ GUE|Γ⁡(s)​Γ​(s+1)​Γ​(s+α)Γ⁡(2​s−1)|2if Xn∼ LUE|Γ⁡(s)​Γ​(s+1)​Γ​(s+α2)Γ⁡(s+α1+α2+2​n)​Γ​(2​s−1)|2if Xn∼ JUE,w(s)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l@{\quad}cr}\displaystyle\left|2\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(2s)\right|^{2}&\text{if $X_{n}\sim$ GUE}\\ \\ \displaystyle\left|\frac{\Gamma(s)\Gamma(s+1)\Gamma(s+\alpha)}{\Gamma(2s-1)}\right|^{2}&\text{if $X_{n}\sim$ LUE}\\ \\ \displaystyle\left|\frac{\Gamma(s)\Gamma(s+1)\Gamma(s+\alpha_{2})}{\Gamma(s+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n)\Gamma(2s-1)}\right|^{2}&\text{if $X_{n}\sim$ JUE}\ ,\end{array}\right.

For the GUE and LUE, the following orthogonality conditions hold

(4.1) 12​π​i​∫12+i​ℝ+ξm​(s)​ξn¯​(s)​w​(s)​𝑑s=hm​δm​n,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int\limits_{\frac{1}{2}+i\mathbb{R}_{+}}\xi_{m}(s)\overline{\xi_{n}}(s)w(s)ds=h_{m}\;\delta_{mn},

where hmh_{m} is an explicit constant depending on the ensemble (see Appendix C).

For an illustration of the zeros on the critical line, see Fig 2 and 3. For the reader’s convenience, the relation between moments of the unitary ensembles and hypergeometric OP’s is summarised in Table 1.

Remark.

The orthogonality in the JUE is slightly different to the GUE and LUE cases. First of all, the fourth parameter of the Wilson polynomial is negative. An orthogonality relation in this case is far from obvious and was established by Neretin [67], see also Appendix C. This fourth parameter also depends on nn, therefore each ξn​(s)\xi_{n}(s) belongs to a distinct family of orthogonal polynomials obtained by fixing the fourth parameter. As before, this orthogonality implies that the zeros lie on the line Re⁡(s)=1/2\mathrm{Re}(s)=1/2.

4.1. Gaussian Unitary Ensemble

The GUE is a classical orthogonal polynomial ensemble. In particular, the correlation functions can be compactly and conveniently written in terms of Hermite polynomials. It turns out that the complex moments are essentially a Meixner-Pollaczek polynomial. The moments for GOE and GSE can be expressed using known formulae relating the one-point correlation functions of the three Gaussian ensembles.

Let XnX_{n} be a GUE random matrix of dimension nn. Define Qkℂ​(n)=𝔼​Tr⁡Xn2​kQ_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{2k} for all k∈ℂk\in\mathbb{C} for which the expectation exists. It is known [46] that, for k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N},

(4.2) Qkℂ​(n)=(2​k−1)!!​∑i=1n2i−1​(ni)​(ki−1),Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)=(2k-1)!!\sum_{i=1}^{n}2^{i-1}\binom{n}{i}\binom{k}{i-1},

where (2​k−1)!!=2k​Γ​(1/2+k)/π(2k-1)!!=2^{k}\Gamma(1/2+k)/\sqrt{\pi} (this is equal to (2k−1)(2k−3)⋯1(2k-1)(2k-3)\cdots 1 for k≥1k\geq 1 integer). For each kk, the moment Qkℂ​(n)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n) is a polynomial in nn with positive integer coefficients:

Q0ℂ​(n)\displaystyle Q_{0}^{\mathbb{C}}(n) =n\displaystyle=n
Q1ℂ​(n)\displaystyle Q_{1}^{\mathbb{C}}(n) =n2\displaystyle=n^{2}
Q2ℂ​(n)\displaystyle Q_{2}^{\mathbb{C}}(n) =2​n3+n\displaystyle=2n^{3}+n
Q3ℂ​(n)\displaystyle Q_{3}^{\mathbb{C}}(n) =5​n4+10​n2.\displaystyle=5n^{4}+10n^{2}.
Q4ℂ​(n)\displaystyle Q_{4}^{\mathbb{C}}(n) =14​n5+70​n3+21​n.\displaystyle=14n^{5}+70n^{3}+21n.

This fact is the well-known genus expansion for Gaussian complex matrices.

As observed in [75, Theorem 8],  (4.2) can be written in terms of a (terminating) hypergeometric series:

(4.3) Qkℂ​(n)n⁡(2​k−1)!!=F12​(−k,1−n2,2).\frac{Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)}{n\;(2k-1)!!}=\;{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}-k,1-n\\ 2\end{matrix};2\right).

From this hypergeometric representation, we see that the moment Qkℂ​(n)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n), if properly normalised, is a Meixner-Pollaczek polynomial in i⁡(k+1)i(k+1) of degree n−1n-1.

Theorem 4.2.

If we write x=i⁡(k+1)x=i(k+1), then for Re(k)>−1/2\operatorname{Re}(k)>-1/2

(4.4) Qkℂ​(n)=i1−n​(2​k−1)!!​Pn−1(1)​(x,π/2)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)=i^{1-n}\;(2k-1)!!\;P^{(1)}_{n-1}(x;\;\pi/2)

In particular, in−1​Qkℂ​(n)/(2​k−1)!!i^{n-1}Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)/(2k-1)!! can be extended to an analytic function in ℂ\mathbb{C} (a polynomial), invariant up to a change of sign under reflection k→−2−kk\to-2-k, with complex zeros on the vertical line Re⁡(k)=−1\operatorname{Re}(k)=-1.

Consider the polynomials

qr​(s)=i−r1+r​Pr(1)​(i​s,π/2).q_{r}(s)=\frac{i^{-r}}{1+r}P_{r}^{(1)}(is;\ \pi/2).

From the definition of Meixner-Pollaczek polynomials (3.15) of Pn−1(1)​(x,π/2)P^{(1)}_{n-1}(x;\;\pi/2) and the hypergeometric representation (4.3) we see that Qkℂ​(n)=n⁡(2​k−1)!!​qk​(n)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)=n\;(2k-1)!!\;q_{k}(n) when kk is a nonnegative integer. In order to prove the general complex case, we use a procedure of analytic continuation from integer points to a complex domain via Carlson’s theorem [7, Theorem 2.8.1]. A standard calculation in random matrix theory shows that, for Re(k)>−1/2\operatorname{Re}(k)>-1/2,

=∑j=0n−1dj​2k+j−1π​Γ​(k+j+1/2)\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}d_{j}\frac{2^{k+j-1}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\Gamma(k+j+1/2)
=2kπ​Γ​(k+1/2)​∑j=0n−1dj​2j−1​∏i=0j−1(k+1/2+i).\displaystyle=\frac{2^{k}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\Gamma(k+1/2)\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}d_{j}2^{j-1}\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(k+1/2+i).

Therefore in−1​Qkℂ​(n)/(2​k−1)!!=O⁡(kn−1)i^{n-1}Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)/(2k-1)!!=\operatorname{O}(k^{n-1}) as |k|→∞|k|\to\infty with Re(k)>−1/2\operatorname{Re}(k)>-1/2. In conclusion, Qkℂ​(n)/(2​k−1)!!Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)/(2k-1)!! and the polynomial Pn−1(1)​(i⁡(k+1),π/2)P^{(1)}_{n-1}(i(k+1);\;\pi/2) coincide on nonnegative integers and their difference is O⁡(ec​|k|)\operatorname{O}(e^{c|k|}) for any c>0c>0. By Carlson’s theorem the two functions coincide in the whole domain Re(k)>−1/2\operatorname{Re}(k)>-1/2.

The polynomials qr​(s)q_{r}(s) enjoy the symmetries

qr−1​(s)\displaystyle q_{r-1}(s) =qs−1​(r)\displaystyle=q_{s-1}(r)
qr​(−s)\displaystyle q_{r}(-s) =(−1)r​qr​(s).\displaystyle=(-1)^{r}q_{r}(s).

Therefore Qkℂ​(n)=n⁡(2​k−1)!!​qn−1​(k+1)=n⁡(2​k−1)!!​(−1)n−1​qn−1​(−k−1)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)=n\;(2k-1)!!\;q_{n-1}(k+1)=n\;(2k-1)!!\;(-1)^{n-1}q_{n-1}(-k-1) thus explaining the reflection symmetry k→−2−kk\to-2-k. Recall that the Meixner-Pollaczek polynomial form an orthogonal family with respect to a positive weight on the real line. Therefore, the zeros of qr​(s)q_{r}(s) are purely imaginary; they occur in conjugate pairs, with zero included if rr is odd. This proves that all the zeros of in−1​Qkℂ​(n)/(2​k−1)!!i^{n-1}Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)/(2k-1)!! lie on the line Re⁡(k)=−1\operatorname{Re}(k)=-1. ∎

Remark.

The polynomials qr​(s)q_{r}(s) satisfy the difference equation

(s+1)​qr​(s+1)=2​(r+1)​qr​(s)+(s−1)​qr​(s−1),(s+1)q_{r}(s+1)=2(r+1)q_{r}(s)+(s-1)q_{r}(s-1),

and the three-term recurrence

(r+2)​qr+1​(s)=2​s​qr​(s)+r​qr−1​(s).(r+2)q_{r+1}(s)=2sq_{r}(s)+rq_{r-1}(s).

Since qr−1​(s)=qs−1​(r)q_{r-1}(s)=q_{s-1}(r), these are in fact equivalent.

Recalling that Qkℂ​(n)=n⁡(2​k−1)!!​qk​(n),Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)=n\;(2k-1)!!\;q_{k}(n), this yields the Harer-Zagier recursion [46]

(4.5) (k+2)​Qk+1ℂ​(n)=2​n​(2​k+1)​Qkℂ​(n)+k⁡(2​k+1)​(2​k−1)​Qk−1ℂ​(n),(k+2)Q_{k+1}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)=2n(2k+1)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)+k(2k+1)(2k-1)Q_{k-1}^{\mathbb{C}}(n),

and the recursion in nn

(4.6) n​Qkℂ​(n+1)=2​(k+1)​Qkℂ​(n)+n​Qkℂ​(n−1).nQ_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n+1)=2(k+1)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)+nQ_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n-1).

The Meixner-Pollaczek polynomials can be thought as continuous version of the Meixer polynomials [9]:

Pn(λ)​(x,ϕ)=e−i​n​ϕ​(2​λ)nn!​Mn​(−λ+i​x, 2​λ,e−2​i​ϕ).P_{n}^{(\lambda)}(x;\;\phi)=e^{-in\phi}\frac{(2\lambda)_{n}}{n!}M_{n}(-\lambda+ix;\;2\lambda,e^{-2i\phi}).

In fact, the normalized moment (4.3) is a Meixner polynomial (see (3.11)) in n−1n-1 of degree kk or, by symmetry, a Meixner polynomial in kk of degree n−1n-1. The alternative form of Theorem 4.2 using Meixner polynomials is the following.

Theorem 4.2′.
(4.7) Qkℂ​(n)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n) =n⁡(2​k−1)!!​Mk​(n−1,2,−1)=n⁡(2​k−1)!!​Mn−1​(k,2,−1).\displaystyle=n\;(2k-1)!!\;M_{k}(n-1;2,-1)=n\;(2k-1)!!\;M_{n-1}(k;2,-1).

The first polynomials are

Qkℂ​(1)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(1) =(2​k−1)!!\displaystyle=\;(2k-1)!!
Qkℂ​(2)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(2) =2​(2​k−1)!!⋅(k+1)\displaystyle=2(2k-1)!!\cdot\left(k+1\right)
Qkℂ​(3)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(3) =3​(2​k−1)!!⋅13​(2​k2+4​k+3)\displaystyle=3(2k-1)!!\cdot\frac{1}{3}\left(2k^{2}+4k+3\right)
Qkℂ​(4)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(4) =4​(2​k−1)!!⋅13​(k3+3​k2+5​k+3)\displaystyle=4(2k-1)!!\cdot\frac{1}{3}\left(k^{3}+3k^{2}+5k+3\right)
Qkℂ​(5)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(5) =5​(2​k−1)!!⋅115​(2​k4+8​k3+22​k2+28​k+15).\displaystyle=5(2k-1)!!\cdot\frac{1}{15}\left(2k^{4}+8k^{3}+22k^{2}+28k+15\right).
Remark.

The normalised GUE moments can be written as products of moments (2​k−1)!!(2k-1)!! of a standard Gaussian, times a Meixner polynomial

1n​Qkℂ​(n)=(2​k−1)!!​Mk​(n−1, 2,−1).\frac{1}{n}Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)=(2k-1)!!\;M_{k}(n-1;\;2,-1).

It is natural to ask whether the Meixner polynomials form moment sequences of some random variables, so that one can ‘decompose’ the GUE one-point function as multiplicative convolution of a standard Gaussian and another probability distribution (product of two independent random variables). In fact, Ismail and Stanton [47] considered the problem of orthogonal polynomials as moments. It turns out that the Meixner polynomials are moments of translated Beta random variables

(1−c)1−β​Γ⁡(β)Γ⁡(x+β)​Γ​(−x)​∫c1tk​(1−t)x+β−1​(t−c)−x−1​𝑑t=cn​Mk​(x,β,c),(1-c)^{1-\beta}\frac{\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(x+\beta)\Gamma(-x)}\int_{c}^{1}t^{k}\;(1-t)^{x+\beta-1}(t-c)^{-x-1}dt=c^{n}M_{k}(x;\beta,c),

for Re⁡(x)<0\operatorname{Re}(x)<0 and Re⁡(x+β)>0\operatorname{Re}(x+\beta)>0. Note however that, in our setting, the Meixner polynomials have nonnegative argument x=n−1x=n-1, so that this representation of the one-point function as a ‘convolution’ is purely formal.

As a corollary of Theorem 4.2 we have the following two identities.

Corollary 4.3.

Reflection formula:

(4.8) 1n​1(2​k−1)!!​Qkℂ​(n)=1k+1​1(2​(n−1)−1)!!​Qn−1ℂ​(k+1).\frac{1}{n}\frac{1}{(2k-1)!!}Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)=\frac{1}{k+1}\frac{1}{(2(n-1)-1)!!}Q_{n-1}^{\mathbb{C}}(k+1).

Convolution formula:

(4.9) ∑j=0k(j+1)(2​j−1)!!​(k−j+1)(2​(k−j)−1)!!​Qjℂ​(n)n​Qk−jℂ​(n)n=14​1(2​(k+2)−1)!!​(Qk+2ℂ​(2​n+1)2​n+1​(k+2−2​n)+Qk+2ℂ​(2​n−1)2​n−1​(k+2+2​n)).\sum_{j=0}^{k}\frac{(j+1)}{(2j-1)!!}\frac{(k-j+1)}{(2(k-j)-1)!!}\frac{Q_{j}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)}{n}\frac{Q_{k-j}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)}{n}\\ =\frac{1}{4}\frac{1}{(2(k+2)-1)!!}\left(\frac{Q_{k+2}^{\mathbb{C}}(2n+1)}{2n+1}(k+2-2n)+\frac{Q_{k+2}^{\mathbb{C}}(2n-1)}{2n-1}(k+2+2n)\right).
Proof.

The reflection formula follows from the hypergeometric representation in (4.3). To prove (4.9) we start from the convolution property of the Meixner-Pollaczek polynomials [5]

Pk(λ+μ)​(x+y,ϕ)=∑j=0kPj(λ)​(x,ϕ)​Pk−j(μ)​(y,ϕ).P^{(\lambda+\mu)}_{k}(x+y;\;\phi)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}P^{(\lambda)}_{j}(x;\;\phi)P^{(\mu)}_{k-j}(y;\;\phi).

It follows that

∑j=0k(i/2)j​π​(j+1)Γ⁡(j+1/2)​Qjℂ​(n)​(i/2)k−j​π​(k−j+1)Γ⁡(k−j+1/2)​Qk−jℂ​(n)=Pk(2)​(2​i​n,π/2).\sum_{j=0}^{k}\frac{(i/2)^{j}\sqrt{\pi}(j+1)}{\Gamma(j+1/2)}Q_{j}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)\frac{(i/2)^{k-j}\sqrt{\pi}(k-j+1)}{\Gamma(k-j+1/2)}Q_{k-j}^{\mathbb{C}}(n)=P^{(2)}_{k}(2in;\;\pi/2).

To complete the proof we use the Forward Shift Operator for the Meixner-Pollaczek polynomials[48, Sec. 9, Eq. (9.7.6)], the reflection formula (4.8), and the recursion (4.6). ∎

Remark.

The reflection formula (4.8) relates expectations of power of traces when the role of kk and nn is interchanged. We remark that these are not the only quantities invariant under this type of reflection. The other main examples are moments of characteristic polynomials. See the work of Mehta and Normand [59, Eq. (3.15)] and Forrester and Witte [34, Eq. (4.43)]. A generalization of such a duality to all β\beta was obtained in the work of Desrosiers [30].

4.2. Laguerre unitary ensemble

The moments of the Laguerre polynomial ensemble (LUE) enjoy a polynomial property, too. They are (dual) Hahn polynomials (3.9)-(3.10), or their continuous versions (3.13)-(3.14).

Let XnX_{n} be a LUE random matrix with parameter mm. Denote α=m−n≥0\alpha=m-n\geq 0. Set Qkℂ​(m,n)=𝔼​Tr⁡XnkQ_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k} for all k∈ℂk\in\mathbb{C} for which the expectation exists. Then Q0ℂ​(m,n)=nQ_{0}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=n and, for k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, it is known that [45]

(4.10) Qkℂ​(m,n)=1k​∑i=1k(−1)i−1​(m−i+1)k​(n−i+1)k(k−i)!​(i−1)!.Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}(-1)^{i-1}\frac{(m-i+1)_{k}(n-i+1)_{k}}{(k-i)!(i-1)!}.

For any k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, Qkℂ​(m,n)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n) is a symmetric polynomial in m,nm,n of degree k+1k+1, with positive integer coefficients:

Q1ℂ​(m,n)\displaystyle Q_{1}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n) =m​n\displaystyle=mn
Q2ℂ​(m,n)\displaystyle Q_{2}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n) =m2​n+m​n2\displaystyle=m^{2}n+mn^{2}
Q3ℂ​(m,n)\displaystyle Q_{3}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n) =m3​n+3​m2​n2+m​n3+m​n\displaystyle=m^{3}n+3m^{2}n^{2}+mn^{3}+mn
Q4ℂ​(m,n)\displaystyle Q_{4}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n) =m4​n+6​m3​n2+6​m2​n3+m​n4+5​m2​n+5​m​n2.\displaystyle=m^{4}n+6m^{3}n^{2}+6m^{2}n^{3}+mn^{4}+5m^{2}n+5mn^{2}.

In fact, for each positive integer nn, Qkℂ​(m,n)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n) is a polynomial in kk of degree 2​(n−1)2(n-1). After some manipulations, the moments (4.10) can be expressed in terms of a hypergeometric function:

(4.11) Qkℂ​(m,n)(k+α)!=m​n(1+α)!​F23​(1−k,2+k,1−n2,2+α,1).\frac{Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)}{(k+\alpha)!}=\frac{mn}{(1+\alpha)!}\;{}_{3}F_{2}\left(\begin{matrix}1-k,2+k,1-n\\ 2,2+\alpha\end{matrix};1\right).

This formula can be extended for k∈ℂk\in\mathbb{C} and satisfies Q0ℂ​(m,n)=nQ_{0}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=n.

Theorem 4.4.

If we write k=i​x−1/2k=ix-1/2, then for Re⁡(k)>−α−1\operatorname{Re}(k)>-\alpha-1,

(4.12) Qkℂ​(m,n)=(k+α)!(n−1)!​(m−1)!​Sn−1​(x2,32,12,α+12),Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=\frac{(k+\alpha)!}{(n-1)!\;(m-1)!}S_{n-1}\left(x^{2};\;\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2},\alpha+\frac{1}{2}\right),

where Sn−1S_{n-1} denotes the continuous dual Hahn polynomial of degree n−1n-1. In particular this shows that Qkℂ​(m,n)/(k+α)!Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)/(k+\alpha)! can be extended to a polynomial invariant under the reflection k→−1−kk\to-1-k (reciprocity law) and, moreover, its complex zeros lie on the critical line Re(k)=−1/2\operatorname{Re}(k)=-1/2.

Proof.

Comparing (4.11) with the hypergeometric representation of continuous dual Hahn polynomials (3.13) we get the result for kk integer. The extension to complex kk is again an application of Carlson’s theorem. ∎

An alternative formulation in terms of Hahn and dual Hahn polynomials (3.9)-(3.10) is as follows.

Theorem 4.4′.
(4.13) Qkℂ​(m,n)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n) =m​n​(2+α)k−1​Rn−1​((k−1)​(k+2), 1,1,−2−α)\displaystyle=mn(2+\alpha)_{k-1}R_{n-1}((k-1)(k+2);\;1,1,-2-\alpha)
(4.14) =m​n​(2+α)k−1​Qk−1​(n−1, 1,1,−2−α).\displaystyle=mn(2+\alpha)_{k-1}Q_{k-1}(n-1;\;1,1,-2-\alpha).
Remark.

The difference equations / three-term recurrence relations for these polynomials (see [48, Sections 9.5 and 9.6]) yield the Haagerup-Thorbjørnsen recursion [44, 28]

(4.15) (k+2)​Qk+1ℂ​(m,n)=(2​k+1)​(2​n+α)​Qkℂ​(m,n)+(k−1)​(k2−α2)​Qk−1ℂ​(m,n).(k+2)Q_{k+1}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=(2k+1)(2n+\alpha)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)+(k-1)(k^{2}-\alpha^{2})Q_{k-1}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n).

If kk is a positive integer, and we treat α\alpha as a parameter, then Qkℂ​(m,n)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n) is a polynomial in nn of degree k+1k+1. Moreover, we can write

(4.16) Qkℂ​(m,n)=i1−kk​n​(n+α)​pk−1​(i​n,1,1−α,1,1+α),Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=\frac{i^{1-k}}{k}n(n+\alpha)p_{k-1}(in;1,1-\alpha,1,1+\alpha),

where pk−1p_{k-1} denotes the continuous Hahn polynomial (3.14) of degree k−1k-1.

Note the alternative formula:

Qkℂ​(m,n)=k!​(n+k−1n−1)​(m+k−1m−1)​F23​(1−k,1−n,1−m1−k−n,1−k−m,1).Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=k!\binom{n+k-1}{n-1}\binom{m+k-1}{m-1}\;{}_{3}F_{2}\left(\begin{matrix}1-k,1-n,1-m\\ 1-k-n,1-k-m\end{matrix};1\right).

If α\alpha is fixed and we write Qkℂ​(m,n)=an​RnQ_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=a_{n}R_{n}, where an=n⁡(n+α)a_{n}=n(n+\alpha), then

(k−1)​(k+2)​Rn=an+1​Rn+1−(an+1+an−1)​Rn+an−1​Rn−1.(k-1)(k+2)R_{n}=a_{n+1}R_{n+1}-(a_{n+1}+a_{n-1})R_{n}+a_{n-1}R_{n-1}.

It is very natural to consider mm dependent on nn. An interesting situation (from the point of view of the large-nn limit) is the case m=c​nm=cn with c>0c>0 and fixed. The next result shows that the moments, as functions of nn, are polynomials with all zeros on a vertical line in the complex plane.

Lemma 4.5.

Let m=c​nm=cn and kk a positive integer. Then, n−(k+1)​Qkℂ​(c​n,n)n^{-(k+1)}Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(cn,n) is a polynomial in n−2n^{-2} of degree ⌊(k−1)/2⌋\lfloor(k-1)/2\rfloor with positive coefficients.

Proof.

From [45, Corollary 2.4] we have

(4.17) 1nk+1​Qkℂ​(c​n,n)=∑σ∈Skc#⁡(σ)​n#⁡(σ)+#⁡(γk​σ−1)−(k+1).\frac{1}{n^{k+1}}Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(cn,n)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{k}}c^{\#(\sigma)}n^{\#(\sigma)+\#(\gamma_{k}\sigma^{-1})-(k+1)}.

For any permutation σ∈Sk\sigma\in S_{k}, one has

(−1)k−#⁡(σ)=sgn⁡(σ)(-1)^{k-\#(\sigma)}=\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)

Hence

(−1)k−#⁡(σ)+k−#⁡(γk​σ−1)=sgn⁡(σ)​sgn​(γk​σ−1)=sgn⁡(γk)=(−1)k+1(-1)^{k-\#(\sigma)+k-\#(\gamma_{k}\sigma^{-1})}=\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\mathrm{sgn}(\gamma_{k}\sigma^{-1})=\mathrm{sgn}(\gamma_{k})=(-1)^{k+1}

and so

(−1)#⁡(σ)+#⁡(γk​σ−1)=(−1)k+1(-1)^{\#(\sigma)+\#(\gamma_{k}\sigma^{-1})}=(-1)^{k+1}

Hence #⁡(σ)+#⁡(γk​σ−1)−(k+1)\#(\sigma)+\#(\gamma_{k}\sigma^{-1})-(k+1) is even and (4.17) is a polynomial in n−2n^{-2}. ∎

Theorem 4.6.

Fix c>0c>0. The zeros of the polynomials Qkℂ​(c​n,n)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(cn,n) as a function of nn are purely imaginary and satisfy the interlacing property.

Proof.

Let qk​(n)=Qkℂ​(c​n,n)/nq_{k}(n)=Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(cn,n)/n. Then for each kk, qk​(n)q_{k}(n) is a polynomial of degree kk, with positive coefficients, and only powers nk,nk−2,…n^{k},n^{k-2},\dots (see Lemma 4.5). It follows that if we define pk​(x)=ik​qk​(−i​x)p_{k}(x)=i^{k}q_{k}(-ix), then pk​(x)p_{k}(x) is a polynomial of degree kk, with alternating signs, and satisfies the (Haagerup-Thorbjørnsen) recursion

(4.18) (k+1)​pk​(x)=(c+1)​(2​k−1)​x​pk−1​(x)−(k−2)​((k−1)2+(c−1)2​x2)​pk−2​(x).(k+1)p_{k}(x)=(c+1)(2k-1)xp_{k-1}(x)-(k-2)((k-1)^{2}+(c-1)^{2}x^{2})p_{k-2}(x).

It now follows from [55, Corollary 2.4] that {pk​(x)}\{p_{k}(x)\} is a ‘Sturm sequence’ of polynomials. Hence the pkp_{k}’s have only real zeros, and they satisfy the interlacing property. ∎

4.3. Jacobi unitary ensemble

Let XnX_{n} be a JUE random matrix of size nn with parameters α1=m1−n\alpha_{1}=m_{1}-n, α2=m2−n\alpha_{2}=m_{2}-n. It turns out that the suitable statistics in this ensemble are differences of consecutive moments Δ​Qkℂ​(α1,α2,n)\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n), defined as

Qkℂ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k}
Δ​Qkℂ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =Qkℂ​(α1,α2,n)−Qk+1ℂ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle=Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)-Q_{k+1}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)

for all k∈ℂk\in\mathbb{C} for which the expectations exist.

Theorem 4.7.

In terms of Wilson polynomials, writing k=i​x−1/2k=ix-1/2, for Re⁡(k)>−α2−1\operatorname{Re}(k)>-\alpha_{2}-1,

(4.19) Δ​Qkℂ​(α1,α2,n)=(k+α2)!(k+α1+α2+2​n)!​(α1+n)​(α1+α2+n)!(n−1)!​(α2+n−1)!(−1)n−1​Wn−1​(x2,32,12,α2+12,12−α1−α2−2​n).\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)=\frac{(k+\alpha_{2})!}{(k+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n)!}\frac{(\alpha_{1}+n)\;(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+n)!}{(n-1)!\;(\alpha_{2}+n-1)!}\\ (-1)^{n-1}W_{n-1}\left(x^{2};\;\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2},\alpha_{2}+\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}-2n\right).

This shows that Δ​Qkℂ​(α1,α2,n)​((k+α1+α2)!/(k+α1)!)\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)((k+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})!/(k+\alpha_{1})!) can be extended to a polynomial invariant under the reflection k→−1−kk\to-1-k (reciprocity law) and, moreover, its complex zeros lie on the critical line Re(k)=−1/2\operatorname{Re}(k)=-1/2.

In this case, our strategy is to look for a three-term recursion for Δ​Qkℂ​(α1,α2,n)\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) when kk is an integer. In fact, adapting a method due to Ledoux [52, Eq. (30)-(31)], we find the following recurrence relation for the JUE which is the analogue of the Harer-Zagier and Haagerup-Thorbjørnsen recursions.

Proposition 4.8 (Three term recurrence relation for JUE).

Let k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}. Then,

(4.20) Rk​Δ​Qk+1ℂ​(α1,α2,n)+Sk​Δ​Qkℂ​(α1,α2,n)+Tk​Δ​Qk−1ℂ​(α1,α2,n)=0,\displaystyle R_{k}\Delta Q_{k+1}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)+S_{k}\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)+T_{k}\Delta Q_{k-1}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)=0,

with ‘initial conditions’

(4.21) Δ​Q0ℂ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle\Delta Q_{0}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =n⁡(α1+n)α1+α2+2​n\displaystyle=\frac{n(\alpha_{1}+n)}{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n}
(4.22) Δ​Q1ℂ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle\Delta Q_{1}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =n⁡(α1+α2+n)​(α1+n)​(α2+n)(α1+α2+2​n−1)​(α1+α2+2​n)​(α1+α2+2​n+1).\displaystyle=\frac{n(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+n)(\alpha_{1}+n)(\alpha_{2}+n)}{(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n-1)(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n)(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n+1)}.

The coefficient RkR_{k}, SkS_{k}, and TkT_{k} are given by

Rk​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle R_{k}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =(k+2)​((α1+α2+2​n)2−(k+1)2),\displaystyle=(k+2)((\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n)^{2}-(k+1)^{2}),
Sk​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle S_{k}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =−(2​k+1)​(2​n​(α1+α2+n)+α22+α1​α2−k⁡(k+1)),\displaystyle=-(2k+1)(2n(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+n)+\alpha_{2}^{2}+\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}-k(k+1)),

Proof of Theorem 4.7.

The proof is immediate when kk is a nonnegative integer by observing that (4.20) is the discrete S-L problem for Wilson polynomials, and by checking the initial conditions. For kk complex we can use the same method of Theorem 4.2. ∎

Remark.

Using the hypergeometric representation of Wilson polynomials (3.12) we have the explicit formula

Δ​Qkℂ​(α1,α2,n)=Δ​Q1ℂ​(α1,α2,n)​(k+α2)!(1+α2)!​(1+α1+α2+2​n)!(k+α1+α2+2​n)!×F34​(1−k,2+k,1−n,1−n−α12,2+α2,2−α1−α2−2​n,1).\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)=\Delta Q_{1}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)\frac{(k+\alpha_{2})!}{(1+\alpha_{2})!}\frac{(1+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n)!}{(k+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n)!}\\ \times\;{}_{4}F_{3}\left(\begin{matrix}1-k,2+k,1-n,1-n-\alpha_{1}\\ 2,2+\alpha_{2},2-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}-2n\end{matrix};1\right).

To our knowledge, this hypergeometric representation is new.

Remark.

Ledoux [52] obtained a fourth order recursion for moment differences of the Jacobi ensemble, but the ensemble he considers is shifted compared to ours. In our notation, the moments L⁡(k)L(k) considered in [52] can be written as

L⁡(k)=∫01(2​x−1)k​ρn(2)​(x)​𝑑x=∑j=0k(kj)​2j​(−1)k−j​∫01xj​ρn(2)​(x)L(k)=\int_{0}^{1}(2x-1)^{k}\rho^{(2)}_{n}(x)dx=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}2^{j}(-1)^{k-j}\int_{0}^{1}x^{j}\rho^{(2)}_{n}(x)

for which it is shown that L⁡(k)−L⁡(k+2)L(k)-L(k+2) satisfies a fourth order recursion. Using (2​x−1)k−(2​x−1)k+2=4​(2​x−1)k​(x−x2)(2x-1)^{k}-(2x-1)^{k+2}=4(2x-1)^{k}(x-x^{2}) we obtain

L⁡(k)−L⁡(k+2)=∑j=0k(kj)​2j+2​(−1)k−j​Δ​Qj+1ℂ​(α1,α2,n).L(k)-L(k+2)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}2^{j+2}(-1)^{k-j}\Delta Q_{j+1}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n).

It follows that Ledoux’s moment differences can be expressed as a linear combination of hypergeometric functions.

The difference of moments Δ​Qkℂ​(α1,α2,n)\Delta Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) can alternatively be written in terms of Racah polynomials.

Theorem 4.7′.

The JUE difference of moments is (α1+α2+n∉ℤ\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+n\notin\mathbb{Z})

Using the recurrence relation (4.20), one can verify the following identity between positive and negative moments (this is the analogue of (2.3)).

4.4. Generating functions

It is sometimes convenient to define the moments of random matrices in terms of their generating function. The first example of such a generating function was constructed by Harer and Zagier for the GUE of fixed size nn (see Eq. (4.25) below). This convergent series is a rational function. As emphasised by Morozov and Shakirov [65], from the point of view of random matrices and enumeration problems, this is a highly non-trivial result: a generating function for moments at all genera appears to be rational. The generating function of covariances of the GUE computed in [65] turns out to be again an elementary function. The generating function of higher order cumulants of the GUE have been studied recently by Dubrovin and Yang [31] who expressed them in terms of traces of 2×22\times 2 matrix-valued series.

One of the advantages of the representation of the moments in terms of hypergeometric OP’s discussed in the present work, is that we can write explicit formulae for the generating functions of the moments of GUE and LUE for fixed nn and/or kk. Remarkably, these closed expressions are elementary functions.

Proposition 4.10.

Let Qkℂ​(n)Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(n) and Qkℂ​(m,n)Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(m,n) be the moments of the GUE and LUE, respectively. Then

  • GUE:
    (4.25) ∑k=0∞Qkℂ​(n)(2​k−1)!!​tk=12​t​((1+t1−t)n−1)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(n)}{(2k-1)!!}\,t^{k}=\frac{1}{2t}\left(\left(\frac{1+t}{1-t}\right)^{n}-1\right)
    (4.26) ∑n=1∞Qkℂ​(n)(2​k−1)!!​zn=z1−z2​(1+z1−z)k+1\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(n)}{(2k-1)!!}\,z^{n}=\frac{z}{1-z^{2}}\left(\frac{1+z}{1-z}\right)^{k+1}
    (4.27) ∑n≥1,k≥0Qkℂ​(n)(2​k−1)!!​tk​zn=z1−z​1(1−t)−z⁡(1+t).\sum_{n\geq 1,k\geq 0}\frac{Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(n)}{(2k-1)!!}\,t^{k}z^{n}=\frac{z}{1-z}\frac{1}{(1-t)-z(1+t)}.
  • LUE:
    (4.28) ∑k=1∞Qkℂ​(m,n)(k−1)!​tkk!=t​et​Ln−1(1)​(−t)​Lm−1(1)​(−t).\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(m,n)}{(k-1)!}\,\frac{t^{k}}{k!}=te^{t}L_{n-1}^{(1)}(-t)L_{m-1}^{(1)}(-t).
    (4.29) ∑n=1∞Qkℂ​(m,n)​(m−1)!(k+α)!​znn!=z(1−z)α+k+1​F12​(−k,1−k2,z)\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(m,n)\frac{(m-1)!}{(k+\alpha)!}\,\frac{z^{n}}{n!}=\frac{z}{(1-z)^{\alpha+k+1}}\;{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}-k,1-k\\ 2\end{matrix};z\right)
    (4.30) ∑n,m,k≥1Qkℂ​(m,n)(k−1)!​z1n​z2m​tkk!=z1​z2​t(1−z1)2​(1−z2)2​exp⁡(3​z1​z2−2​(z1+z2)+1(1−z1)​(1−z2)​t).\sum_{n,m,k\geq 1}\frac{Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(m,n)}{(k-1)!}\,\frac{z_{1}^{n}z_{2}^{m}t^{k}}{k!}=\frac{z_{1}z_{2}t}{(1-z_{1})^{2}(1-z_{2})^{2}}\,\exp\left(\frac{3z_{1}z_{2}-2(z_{1}+z_{2})+1}{(1-z_{1})(1-z_{2})}t\right).
Proof.

The sum (4.25) can be computed from (4.7) using the formula of the generating function of Meixner polynomials [48, Eq. (9.10.11)]:

∑k=1∞kn​Qkℂ​(n)(2​k−1)!!​tk−1=(1+t1−t)n−1.\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{k}{n}\frac{Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(n)}{(2k-1)!!}t^{k-1}=\left(\frac{1+t}{1-t}\right)^{n-1}.

The formula for generating function (4.25) follows from the identity

nt​dd​t​∑k=0∞Qkℂ​(n)(2​k−1)!!​tk=∑k=1∞kn​Qkℂ​(n)(2​k−1)!!​tk−1.\frac{n}{t}\frac{d}{dt}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(n)}{(2k-1)!!}\,t^{k}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{k}{n}\frac{Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(n)}{(2k-1)!!}t^{k-1}.

The generating function (4.26) for fixed kk, is a direct consequence of the representation of the moments in terms of Meixner-Pollaczek polynomials (4.4) and their generating function [48, Eq. (9.7.11)].

Finally, the joint generating function (4.27) is the resummation in nn of (4.25) (or the resummation in kk of (4.26)).

For the LUE we use the generating series of continuous (dual) Hahn polynomials. From the representation of the LUE moments as continuous Hahn (4.16), using [48, Eq. (9.5.11)] we get

∑k=1∞Qkℂ​(m,n)n​m​(k−1)!​tk−1k!\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(m,n)}{nm\,(k-1)!}\,\frac{t^{k-1}}{k!} =F11​(1−n2,−t)​F11​(1+m2,t)\displaystyle={}_{1}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}1-n\\ 2\end{matrix};-t\right){}_{1}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}1+m\\ 2\end{matrix};t\right)
=F11​(1−n2,−t)​F11​(1−m2,−t)​et.\displaystyle={}_{1}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}1-n\\ 2\end{matrix};-t\right){}_{1}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}1-m\\ 2\end{matrix};-t\right)e^{t}.

Note that the hypergeometric functions on the right-hand side are terminating series. In fact, they are Laguerre polynomials [48, Eq. (9.12.1)], thus proving (4.28).

For (4.29) we use the representation in terms of continuous dual Hahn polynomials (4.12) and the formula of the generating series [48, Eq. (9.3.11)]. We have

∑n=1∞Qkℂ​(m,n)​(m−1)!(k+α)!​znn!=z(1−z)α−k​F12​(k+2,k+12,z),\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(m,n)\frac{(m-1)!}{(k+\alpha)!}\,\frac{z^{n}}{n!}=\frac{z}{(1-z)^{\alpha-k}}\;{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}k+2,k+1\\ 2\end{matrix};z\right),

which is equal to (4.29) by Euler’s tranformation. Note that the hypergeometric series is terminating. In fact, one could also write it in terms of Jacobi polynomials.

The joint generating series in (4.30) is a resummation of (4.28) over nn and mm using the known formula for the generating function of Laguerre polynomials [48, Eq. (9.12.10)]. ∎

Remark.

The series (4.25) was computed by Harer and Zagier [46] using different methods. It is surprising that, although the three-term recurrence in kk and the generating function were known, nobody recognized the moments of the GUE as Meixner polynomials. The generating function of the GUE for fixed kk (Eq. (4.26)) does not seem to appear in the previous literature. The joint series (4.27) appears in the work of Morozov and Shakirov [65] who stressed the nontrivial fact that it is a rational function in both variables.

The generating functions (4.28)-(4.29)-(4.30) for the LUE seem to be new. It is remarkable, again, that these series sum to elementary functions.

5. Large-nn asymptotics of the spectral zeta functions

It is a classical result that, after rescaling, the one-point function ρn(β)​(x)\rho_{n}^{(\beta)}(x) of the random matrix ensembles considered in this paper weakly converges to a compactly supported probability measure, as nn goes to infinity. The limit ρ∞​(x)\rho_{\infty}(x) is known as equilibrium measure of the ensemble and does not depend on the Dyson index β\beta. In formulae, for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N},

limn→∞1nk+1​𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk=∫xk​ρ∞​(x)​𝑑x.\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n^{k+1}}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k}=\int x^{k}\rho_{\infty}(x)dx.

This suggests to define the limit zeta function ζ∞​(s)\zeta_{\infty}(s) as the analytic continuation of ∫|x|−s​ρ∞​(x)​𝑑x\int|x|^{-s}\rho_{\infty}(x)dx. The limit zeta functions for the classical ensembles turn out to be meromorphic functions. For the LUE and JUE, ζ∞​(s)\zeta_{\infty}(s) has infinitely many nontrivial zeros, and they all lie on a critical line.

We discuss the three classical ensembles separately. For notational convenience we consider the GUE, LUE and JUE, although the results hold true for any β\beta-ensemble.

5.1. Gaussian ensemble

The equilibrium measure is given by the semicircular law

(5.1) ρ∞​(x)=12​π​4−x2​ 1x∈(−2,2).\rho_{\infty}(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{4-x^{2}}\;1_{x\in(-2,2)}.

After a suitable rescaling, in the large-nn limit, the integer moments converge to the Catalan numbers:

(5.2) limn→∞1nk+1​Qkℂ​(n)=∫x2​k​ρ∞​(x)​𝑑x=1k+1​(2​kk).\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n^{k+1}}Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(n)=\int x^{2k}\rho_{\infty}(x)dx=\frac{1}{k+1}\binom{2k}{k}.

This formula can be analytically continued and suggests to define the limit GUE zeta function as the analytic continuation of ∫|x|−s​ρ∞​(x)​𝑑x\int|x|^{-s}\rho_{\infty}(x)dx:

(5.3) ζ∞​(s)=2−s​Γ​(1−s2)π​Γ​(2−s2).\zeta_{\infty}(s)=\frac{2^{-s}\;\Gamma\left(\frac{1-s}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\pi}\;\Gamma\left(2-\frac{s}{2}\right)}.

This function has alternating simple poles and zeros on the positive integers, with no other zeros in the rest of the complex plane. The large-nn limit is more interesting for matrices in Laguerre and Jacobi ensembles.

5.2. Laguerre ensemble

Let XnX_{n} be in the Laguerre unitary ensemble. Set α=m−n=(c−1)​n\alpha=m-n=(c-1)n, with c≥1c\geq 1. Define the equilibrium measure

(5.4) ρ∞​(x)=12​π​x​(x+−x)​(x−x−)​ 1x∈(x−,x+)\rho_{\infty}(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi x}\sqrt{(x_{+}-x)(x-x_{-})}\;1_{x\in(x_{-},x_{+})}

where x±=(1±c)2≥0x_{\pm}=(1\pm\sqrt{c})^{2}\geq 0 (this is the celebrated Marchenko-Pastur distribution). Then,

(5.5) limn→∞1nk+1​Qkℂ​((c−1)​n,n)=∫ℝxk​ρ∞​(x)​𝑑x,\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n^{k+1}}Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}((c-1)n,n)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^{k}\rho_{\infty}(x)dx,

Define the limit LUE zeta function as

(5.6) ζ∞​(s)=∫ℝ|x|−s​ρ∞​(x)​d⁡x\zeta_{\infty}(s)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}|x|^{-s}\rho_{\infty}(x)\operatorname{d}x

with ρ∞​(x)\rho_{\infty}(x) in (5.4). From the finite-nn functional equation ξn​(s)=ξn​(1−s)\xi_{n}(s)=\xi_{n}(1-s), we see that a good definition for the limit n→∞n\to\infty is

ξ∞​(s)=(x−​x+)s/2​ζ∞​(s).\xi_{\infty}(s)=(x_{-}x_{+})^{s/2}\zeta_{\infty}(s).
Proposition 5.1.

Assume c>1c>1. Then, the functional equation ξ∞​(s)=ξ∞​(1−s)\xi_{\infty}(s)=\xi_{\infty}(1-s) holds, and the zeros of the ζ∞​(s)\zeta_{\infty}(s) all lie on the critical line Re⁡(s)=1/2\operatorname{Re}(s)=1/2.

Proof.

To prove the functional equation it suffices to use the change of coordinates y=(x+​x−)/xy=(x_{+}x_{-})/x in the integral (5.6), and notice that x−​x+=(c−1)2x_{-}x_{+}=(c-1)^{2}. Alternatively, a calculation using Euler’s integral formula and Pfaff transformation, reveals that

ζ∞​(s)\displaystyle\zeta_{\infty}(s) =116​(x+−x−)2(x−)s+1​F12​(3/2,s+13,x−−x+x−)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{16}\frac{(x_{+}-x_{-})^{2}}{(x_{-})^{s+1}}\;{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}3/2,s+1\\ 3\end{matrix};\frac{x_{-}-x_{+}}{x_{-}}\right)
(5.7) =c​(1−c)−s−1​F12​(34+12​(s−12),34−12​(s−12)2,−4​c(1−c)2).\displaystyle=c(1-c)^{-s-1}\;{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{2}\left(s-\frac{1}{2}\right),\frac{3}{4}-\frac{1}{2}\left(s-\frac{1}{2}\right)\\ 2\end{matrix};-\frac{4c}{(1-c)^{2}}\right).

Then apply Euler’s transformation formula to show the functional equation.

To show that the zeros of ξ∞​(s)\xi_{\infty}(s) are on the critical line we use an argument based on Sturm-Liouville theory (we borrowed this argument from a similar problem in a paper by Biane [16]).

First, observe that the integral (5.6) can not vanish for ss real. We want to show that the zeros of

F12​(34+μ,34−μ2,−4​c(1−c)2),{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}\frac{3}{4}+\mu,\frac{3}{4}-\mu\\ 2\end{matrix};-\frac{4c}{(1-c)^{2}}\right),

where 2​μ=s−1/22\mu=s-1/2, lie on the imaginary axis. The function y⁡(z)=F12​(3/4+μ,3/4−μ,2,−z)y(z)={}_{2}F_{1}(3/4+\mu,3/4-\mu;2;-z) satisfies the hypergeometric equation

z⁡(1+z)​y′′+(2+5​z/2)​y′+(9/16−μ2)​y=0.z(1+z)y^{\prime\prime}+(2+5z/2)y^{\prime}+(9/16-\mu^{2})y=0.

Thus, if μ\mu is such that y⁡(4​c/(1−c)2)=0y(4c/(1-c)^{2})=0, then y⁡(x)y(x) is a solution to the Sturm-Liouville problem

(p⁡(x)​y′​(x))′+q⁡(x)​y​(x)=μ2​w​(x)​y​(x)(p(x)y^{\prime}(x))^{\prime}+q(x)y(x)=\mu^{2}w(x)y(x)

on [4​c/(1−c)2,∞)[4c/(1-c)^{2},\infty), with Dirichlet boundary conditions, where p⁡(x)=x2​(1+x)1/2p(x)=x^{2}(1+x)^{1/2}, q⁡(x)=(9/16)​w​(x)q(x)=(9/16)w(x) and w(x)=x(1+x)−1/2w(x)=x(1+x)^{-1/2}. It then follows from the Sturm-Liouville theory that the eigenvalues μ2\mu^{2} are real which can only happen if μ\mu is real or purely imaginary. Since we have excluded the real case, we conclude that 2​μ=s−1/22\mu=s-1/2 is purely imaginary: the zeros of ζ∞​(s)\zeta_{\infty}(s) all lie on the critical line Re⁡(s)=1/2\operatorname{Re}(s)=1/2. ∎

5.3. Jacobi ensemble

Let XnX_{n} be in the JUE. Set α1,2=(c1,2−1)​n\alpha_{1,2}=(c_{1,2}-1)n, with c1,2≥1c_{1,2}\geq 1. Then, the equilibrium measure is

(5.8) ρ∞​(x)=c1+c22​π​x​(1−x)​(x+−x)​(x−x−)​ 1x∈(x−,x+)\rho_{\infty}(x)=\frac{c_{1}+c_{2}}{2\pi x(1-x)}\sqrt{(x_{+}-x)(x-x_{-})}\;1_{x\in(x_{-},x_{+})}

where x±=(c1±c2​(c1+c2−1)c1+c2)2x_{\pm}=\left(\frac{\sqrt{c_{1}}\pm\sqrt{c_{2}(c_{1}+c_{2}-1)}}{c_{1}+c_{2}}\right)^{2}, and

(5.9) limn→∞1nk+1​Qkℂ​((c1−1)​n,(c2−1)​n,n)=∫ℝxk​(1−x)​ρ∞​(x)​d⁡x\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n^{k+1}}Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}((c_{1}-1)n,(c_{2}-1)n,n)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^{k}(1-x)\rho_{\infty}(x)\operatorname{d}x

Define the limit JUE zeta function as

(5.10) ζ∞​(s)=∫ℝ|x|−s​ρ∞​(x)​d⁡x\zeta_{\infty}(s)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}|x|^{-s}\rho_{\infty}(x)\operatorname{d}x

with ρ∞​(x)\rho_{\infty}(x) in (5.8). Again, the finite-nn functional equation ξn​(s)=ξn​(1−s)\xi_{n}(s)=\xi_{n}(1-s), suggests the definition of

ξ∞​(s)=(x−​x+)s/2​(ζ∞​(s)−ζ∞​(s−1)).\xi_{\infty}(s)=(x_{-}x_{+})^{s/2}\left(\zeta_{\infty}(s)-\zeta_{\infty}(s-1)\right).
Proposition 5.2.

The proof of Proposition 5.1 is easily adapted. ∎

6. Beyond random matrices: Wronskians of orthogonal polynomials

6.1. Mellin transform of orthogonal polynomials

Bump and Ng [20] and Bump, Choi, Kurlberg and Vaaler [21] made the remarkable discovery that the Mellin transforms of Hermite and Laguerre functions have zeros on the critical line Re⁡(s)=1/2\operatorname{Re}(s)=1/2. Their proof is based on the observation that the Mellin transform preserves orthogonality. Hence, Mellin transforms of orthogonal polynomials are themselves orthogonal with respect to some inner product. Later [23, 24] it was noticed that those orthogonal functions are hypergeometric OP’s (multiplied by some nonnegative integrable weight).

Consider, for concreteness, the Hermite polynomials Hn​(x)H_{n}(x) and the normalised Hermite wavefunctions ϕn(x)=(2nn!π)−1/2e−x2/2Hn(x)\phi_{n}(x)=(2^{n}n!\sqrt{\pi})^{-1/2}e^{-x^{2}/2}H_{n}(x). The following proposition follows from the result of Bump et al. [20, 21].

Proposition 6.1 (Mellin transform of Hermite functions).

For all integers n≥0n\geq 0

ϕ2​n∗​(s)\displaystyle\phi_{2n}^{*}(s) =in​2n−1+s2​n!(2​n)!​π​Γ​(s2)​Pn(14)​(−i​(s−1/2)2,π2)\displaystyle=i^{n}2^{n-1+\frac{s}{2}}\frac{n!}{\sqrt{(2n)!\sqrt{\pi}}}\Gamma\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)P^{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}_{n}\left(-i\frac{(s-1/2)}{2};\;\frac{\pi}{2}\right)
ϕ2​n+1∗​(s)\displaystyle\phi_{2n+1}^{*}(s) =in​2n+s2​n!(2​n+1)!​π​Γ​(s+12)​Pn(34)​(−i​(s−1/2)2,π2).\displaystyle=i^{n}2^{n+\frac{s}{2}}\frac{n!}{\sqrt{(2n+1)!\sqrt{\pi}}}\Gamma\left(\frac{s+1}{2}\right)P^{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}_{n}\left(-i\frac{(s-1/2)}{2};\;\frac{\pi}{2}\right).

The averaged spectral zeta function of unitary invariant ensembles of random matrices can be interpreted as Mellin transform of Wronskians of adjacent Hermite, Laguerre or Jacobi wavefunctions. Given our results, it is natural to ask whether more general Wronskians have the property that their Mellin transforms can be written in terms of hypergeometric OP’s.

6.2. Mellin transforms of products and Wronskians of classical orthogonal polynomials

In this section we will use repeatedly the properties (B.2)-(B.3)-(B.4) of the Mellin transform.

The Wronskian of smooth functions f1​(x)​…,fm​(x)f_{1}(x)\dots,f_{m}(x) is defined as

Wr⁡(f1​(x),…,fm​(x))=det(fj(i−1)​(x))i,j=1m.\operatorname{Wr}(f_{1}(x),\dots,f_{m}(x))=\det\left(f^{(i-1)}_{j}(x)\right)_{i,j=1}^{m}.

We can also calculate the Mellin transform of a single Jacobi wavefunction in terms of a continuous Hahn polynomial. The interesting case turns out to be for weights with slightly shifted parameters.

Theorem 6.6.

Consider the functions

(6.14) ϕ~n​(x)=xα2−12​(1−x)α1−12​Pn(α1,α2)​(x)​χ[0,1]​(x)\tilde{\phi}_{n}(x)=x^{\frac{\alpha_{2}-1}{2}}(1-x)^{\frac{\alpha_{1}-1}{2}}P^{(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})}_{n}(x)\chi_{[0,1]}(x)

(6.15) ϕ~n∗​(s)=Γ⁡(s+α2−12+n)Γ⁡(s+α1+α22+n)​Γ​(α1+12)​(−i)n×pn(−i(s−1),(α2+1)/2,−(α1+α2)/2−n,(α2+1)/2,−(α1+α2)/2−n).\begin{split}&\tilde{\phi}^{*}_{n}(s)=\frac{\Gamma\left(s+\frac{\alpha_{2}-1}{2}+n\right)}{\Gamma\left(s+\frac{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}{2}+n\right)}\Gamma\left(\frac{\alpha_{1}+1}{2}\right)(-i)^{n}\\ &\times p_{n}(-i(s-1),(\alpha_{2}+1)/2,-(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})/2-n,(\alpha_{2}+1)/2,-(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})/2-n).\end{split}

These polynomials have zeros on the vertical line Re⁡(s)=1\mathrm{Re}(s)=1 and satisfy an orthogonality condition. They are invariant under the reflection s→2−ss\to 2-s (up to a change of sign if nn is odd).

Proof.

To identify the continuous Hahn polynomial, one employs the standard expansion of Jacobi polynomials and calculates the Mellin transform integrating term by term. The result is a hypergeometric sum which can be identified with definition 3.13, leading to (6.15). The difficulty in establishing the conclusion is that these polynomials are only known to be orthogonal when the parameters have positive real part.

We proceed by expressing the right-hand side of (6.15) in terms of Wilson polynomials and apply a result of Neretin [67]. We claim that for generic parameters a,b∈ℂa,b\in\mathbb{C}, we have

(6.16) p2​n​(x,a,b,a,b)\displaystyle p_{2n}(x,a,b,a,b) ∝Wn​(x2,0,1/2,a,b)\displaystyle\propto W_{n}(x^{2},0,1/2,a,b)
(6.17) p2​n+1​(x,a,b,a,b)\displaystyle p_{2n+1}(x,a,b,a,b) ∝x​Wn​(x2,1,1/2,a,b).\displaystyle\propto xW_{n}(x^{2},1,1/2,a,b).

up to a constant independent of xx. If aa and bb have positive real part, this follows by writing the orthogonality condition for the Wilson polynomials with the parameters given in (6.16) or (6.17). Use of the duplication formula for the Gamma function shows that the weight reduces to |Γ⁡(a+i​x)|2​|Γ⁡(b+i​x)|2|\Gamma(a+ix)|^{2}\,|\Gamma(b+ix)|^{2} which is the weight function for continuous Hahn polynomials. If aa or bb have negative real part the identity follows by analytic continuation. Now inserting (6.16) and (6.17) into (6.15) and applying the orthogonality (C.2) completes the proof. ∎

Going back to random matrices, we obtain exact ordinary differential equations for the one-point functions of the classical ensembles. Denote by ρn(2)​(x)\rho_{n}^{(2)}(x) the one-point function of the ensembles GUE, LUE, or JUE. As already discussed in the Introducion, ρn(2)​(x)\rho^{(2)}_{n}(x) can be represented as the Wronskian of two adjacent wavefunctions.

The following proposition is a corollary of the previous theorems on Mellin transforms of Wronskians. For GUE and LUE we recover a result obtained and used earlier by Götze and Tikhomirov [42, Lemma 2.1 and Lemma 3.1]. For the JUE a similar result does not seem to have been published.

Proposition 6.7.

The one-point correlation function ρn(2)​(x)\rho_{n}^{(2)}(x) satisfies the differential equation D​ρn(2)​(x)=0D\rho_{n}^{(2)}(x)=0, where

D​y={y′′′+(4​n−x2)​y′+x​y(GUE)x2​y′′′+4​x​y′′+(x−a)​(b−x)​y′+(1+b2−α2x)​y,(LUE)x2​((1−x)3​y)′′′′+x​((4+x)​(1−x)2​y)′′+(1−x)​A​(x)​y′+B⁡(x)​y,(JUE)\displaystyle Dy=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l@{\quad}cr}\displaystyle y^{\prime\prime\prime}+(4n-x^{2})y^{\prime}+xy&(\mathrm{GUE})\\ \\ \displaystyle x^{2}y^{\prime\prime\prime}+4xy^{\prime\prime}+(x-a)(b-x)y^{\prime}+\left(\frac{1+b}{2}-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{x}\right)y,&(\mathrm{LUE})\\ \\ \displaystyle x^{2}((1-x)^{3}y)^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}+x((4+x)(1-x)^{2}y)^{\prime\prime}+(1-x)A(x)y^{\prime}+B(x)y,&(\mathrm{JUE})\end{array}\right.

where

a=m+n−4​m​n+2,b=m+n+4​m​n+2,a=m+n-\sqrt{4mn+2},\quad b=m+n+\sqrt{4mn+2},

and

A⁡(x)=−((α1+α2)2−2)​x2−4​n​x​(x−1)​(α1+α2+n)+2​α2​x​(α1+α2)−α22+2,A(x)=-\left((\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})^{2}-2\right)x^{2}-4nx(x-1)(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+n)+2\alpha_{2}x(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})-\alpha_{2}^{2}+2,
B⁡(x)=x2​((α1+2​n)2−4)−6​n​x​(α1+n)+2​x−2+α2​(2​x−1)​(x−1)​(α1+2​n)+2​n​(α1+n)−α22x​(1−x)3.B(x)=x^{2}((\alpha_{1}+2n)^{2}-4)-6nx(\alpha_{1}+n)+2x-2\\ +\alpha_{2}(2x-1)(x-1)(\alpha_{1}+2n)+2n(\alpha_{1}+n)-\frac{\alpha_{2}^{2}}{x}(1-x)^{3}.
Proof.

We present the proof for the GUE. The one-point function ρn(2)​(x)\rho^{(2)}_{n}(x) of the GUE is proportional to the Wronskian of consecutive Hermite functions Wn−1,1​(x/2)=Wr⁡(ϕn−1​(x/2),ϕn​(x/2))W_{n-1,1}(x/\sqrt{2})=\operatorname{Wr}(\phi_{n-1}(x/\sqrt{2}),\phi_{n}(x/\sqrt{2})). To prove the Theorem for the GUE it is therefore sufficient to show that the function Wn,1​(x)W_{n,1}(x) satisfies the third-order differential equation

Wn,1′′′​(x)+4​(2​(n+1)−x2)​Wn,1′​(x)+4​x​Wn,1′′′​(x)=0.W_{n,1}^{\prime\prime\prime}(x)+4(2(n+1)-x^{2})W_{n,1}^{\prime}(x)+4xW_{n,1}^{\prime\prime\prime}(x)=0.

The Harer-Zagier recurrence relation (4.5) for the moments of the GUE is in fact a difference equation for the Mellin transform Wn,1∗​(s)W_{n,1}^{*}(s)

(6.18) s⁡(s+1)​(s+2)​Wn,1∗​(s)+8​(s+2)​(n+1)​Wn,1∗​(s+2)−4​(s+5)​Wn,1∗​(s+4)=0,s(s+1)(s+2)W_{n,1}^{*}(s)+8(s+2)(n+1)W_{n,1}^{*}(s+2)-4(s+5)W_{n,1}^{*}(s+4)=0,

Using the properties (B.2)-(B.4) of the Mellin transform we get the claim.

For the LUE and JUE the proof follows the same steps starting from the recurrence relations (4.15) and (4.20). ∎

Remark.

It is natural to ask whether Wronskians of nonadjacent wavefunctions satisfy similar differential equations. The Mellin transforms of those Wronskians are essentially hypergeometric OP’s (see Theorems 6.2, 6.4, and 6.5). Hence, they satisfy a discrete Sturm-Liouville problem. Upon inversion of the Mellin transform this discrete problem correspond to a differential equation.

We discuss, for concreteness the case of Wronskian of Hermite wavefunctions Wn,ℓ​(x)=Wr⁡(ϕn​(x),ϕn+ℓ​(x))W_{n,\ell}(x)=\operatorname{Wr}(\phi_{n}(x),\phi_{n+\ell}(x)). Its Mellin transform is given in (6.2)-(6.3). From the difference equation of Meixner-Pollaczek polynomials

(6.19) (ℓ−s−2)​Pn(ℓ+12)​(−i⁡(s+1)2,π2)−2​(2​n+s+1)​Pn(ℓ+12)​(−i⁡(s+3)2,π2)+(ℓ+s+4)​Pn(ℓ+12)​(−i⁡(s+5)2,π2)=0,(\ell-s-2)P_{n}^{\left(\frac{\ell+1}{2}\right)}\left(-\frac{i(s+1)}{2};\frac{\pi}{2}\right)-2(2n+s+1)P_{n}^{\left(\frac{\ell+1}{2}\right)}\left(-\frac{i(s+3)}{2};\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\\ +(\ell+s+4)P_{n}^{\left(\frac{\ell+1}{2}\right)}\left(-\frac{i(s+5)}{2};\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=0,

the Mellin transform of the Wronskian satisfies the difference equation

(6.20) s⁡(s+1)​(s+2)​(s+3)​(ℓ−s−2)​Wn,ℓ∗​(s)−4​(s+2)​(s+3)​(2​n+ℓ+1)​(s−ℓ+2)​Wn,ℓ∗​(s+2)+4​((s+4)2−ℓ2)​(s−ℓ+2)​Wn,ℓ∗​(s+4)=0.s(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)(\ell-s-2)W_{n,\ell}^{*}(s)-4(s+2)(s+3)(2n+\ell+1)(s-\ell+2)W_{n,\ell}^{*}(s+2)\\ +4((s+4)^{2}-\ell^{2})(s-\ell+2)W_{n,\ell}^{*}(s+4)=0.

This implies that, for generic nn and ℓ\ell, Wn,ℓ​(x)W_{n,\ell}(x) satisfies a fifth-order differential equation. When when ℓ=1\ell=1, formula (6.20) simplifies as (6.18), which corresponds to the third-order equation of Proposition 6.7.

6.3. Convolution of hypergeometric OP’s

If ϕn​(x)\phi_{n}(x) are the Hermite, Laguerre, or Jacobi functions and ωn,ℓ​(x)=ϕn​(x)​ϕn+ℓ​(x)\omega_{n,\ell}(x)=\phi_{n}(x)\phi_{n+\ell}(x), by the convolution property (B.5) of the Mellin transform, we have

(6.21) 12​π​i​∫c−i​∞c+i​∞ϕn∗​(s−u)​ϕn+ℓ∗​(u)​𝑑u=ωn,ℓ∗​(s),\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}\phi_{n}^{*}(s-u)\phi_{n+\ell}^{*}(u)du=\omega_{n,\ell}^{*}(s),

with cc in the fundamental strip of convergence of the Mellin transform. Note that ϕn​(x)\phi_{n}(x) is in L2​(ℝ+)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+}) so that the fundamental strip always contains the line 12+i​ℝ\frac{1}{2}+i\mathbb{R}. Given that ϕn∗\phi_{n}^{*}, ϕn+ℓ∗\phi_{n+\ell}^{*} and ωn,ℓ∗\omega_{n,\ell}^{*} have hypergeometric OP’s factors, the above formula is a ‘convolution formula’ for hypergeoemetric OP’s. Note that this is different from the usual (discrete) convolutions formulas of orthogonal polynomials.

When ϕn​(x)\phi_{n}(x) is a Hermite wavefunction, ϕn∗​(s)\phi_{n}^{*}(s) has a Meixner-Pollaczeck polynomial factor whose parameter depends on the parity of nn. Using the explicit expressions in Proposition 6.1 and Theorem 6.2 we can write the special cases of (6.21):
