7. Higher order cumulants

It is tempting to look for reciprocity formulae for cumulants of higher order (covariances, etc.). Write the moments as Qkℂ​(m,n)=𝔼​Tr⁡XnkQ_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k}, second order moments as Qk,lℂ​(m,n)=𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk​Tr​XnlQ_{k,l}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{l}, and covariances as Ck,lℂ=Qk,lℂ​(m,n)−Qkℂ​(m,n)​Qlℂ​(m,n)C_{k,l}^{\mathbb{C}}=Q_{k,l}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)-Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)Q_{l}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n).

Positive and negative moments of LUE matrices satisfy recursion relations known as loop equations. The following lemma can be proved using standard methods in random matrix theory (see, e.g. [33] for similar loop equations for positive moments of the GUE).

Lemma 7.1 (Loop equations for positive and negative moments of LUE).

For k1,…,kv∈ℕk_{1},\dots,k_{v}\in\mathbb{N}, the positive and negative moments satisfy the relations (loop equations):

(7.1) ∑ℓ=0k1−1𝔼TrXnℓTrXnk1−ℓ+1TrXnk2⋯TrXnkv+∑j=2vkj𝔼TrXnk1+kj−1∏i=2i≠jvTrXnki=𝔼TrXnk1TrXnk2⋯TrXnkv−α𝔼TrXnk1−1TrXnk2⋯TrXnkv,\sum_{\ell=0}^{k_{1}-1}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{\ell}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k_{1}-\ell+1}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k_{2}}\cdots\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k_{v}}+\sum_{j=2}^{v}k_{j}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k_{1}+k_{j}-1}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i=2\\ i\neq j\end{subarray}}^{v}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k_{i}}\\ =\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k_{1}}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k_{2}}\cdots\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k_{v}}-\alpha\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k_{1}-1}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k_{2}}\cdots\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k_{v}},
(7.2) ∑ℓ=0k1−1𝔼TrXn−ℓ−1TrXn−k1+ℓTrXn−k2⋯TrXn−kv+∑j=2vkj𝔼TrXn−k1−kj−1∏i=2i≠jvTrXn−ki=−𝔼TrXn−k1TrXn−k2⋯TrXn−kv+α𝔼TrXn−k1−1TrXn−k2⋯TrXn−kv,\sum_{\ell=0}^{k_{1}-1}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-\ell-1}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k_{1}+\ell}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k_{2}}\cdots\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k_{v}}+\sum_{j=2}^{v}k_{j}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k_{1}-k_{j}-1}\!\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i=2\\ i\neq j\end{subarray}}^{v}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k_{i}}\\ =-\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k_{1}}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k_{2}}\cdots\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k_{v}}+\alpha\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k_{1}-1}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k_{2}}\cdots\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{-k_{v}},

provided they exist.

Proposition 7.2 (Reflection symmetry for LUE covariances).
(7.3) C−k,−1ℂ=Ck,1ℂα2(α2−1)⋯(α2−k2)C_{-k,-1}^{\mathbb{C}}=\frac{C_{k,1}^{\mathbb{C}}}{\alpha^{2}(\alpha^{2}-1)\cdots(\alpha^{2}-k^{2})}

Note that Q0ℂ​(m,n)=nQ_{0}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=n, Q1ℂ​(m,n)=m​nQ_{1}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=mn and Q−1ℂ​(m,n)=n/αQ_{-1}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=n/\alpha. The proof of (7.3) uses the loop equations (7.1)-(7.2) together with the reciprocity law (2.3) for moments, as follows. By the loop equations,

The first gives

Ck,1ℂ=k​Qkℂ​(m,n).C_{k,1}^{\mathbb{C}}=kQ_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n).

Using Q−1ℂ​(m,n)=n/αQ^{\mathbb{C}}_{-1}(m,n)=n/\alpha, the second gives

Q−k,−1ℂ​(m,n)=Q−1ℂ​(m,n)​Q−kℂ​(m,n)+k​Q−k−1ℂ​(m,n)/α,Q_{-k,-1}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)=Q_{-1}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)Q_{-k}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)+kQ_{-k-1}^{\mathbb{C}}(m,n)/\alpha,

There exists also a precise reflection symmetry for the covariances of one-cut β\beta-ensembles at leading order in nn. Suppose that the eigenvalues x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n} of XnX_{n} have a joint probability density proportional to

(7.4) ∏1≤j<k≤n|xk−xj|β​∏i=1ne−n​β​V​(xi)​d​xi(β>0)\prod_{1\leq j<k\leq n}|x_{k}-x_{j}|^{\beta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}e^{-n\beta V(x_{i})}dx_{i}\quad(\beta>0)

The two-point connected correlator

is the generating function of covariances of positive and negative moments

(On the other hand, for multicut ensembles the asymptotics of G2​(z,w)G_{2}(z,w) is more delicate due to the presence of oscillating terms [2, 12]). In the Laguerre ensemble set α=m−n=(c−1)​n\alpha=m-n=(c-1)n, with c>1c>1. The edges x±x_{\pm} of the cut are strictly positive, see (5.4). In the Jacobi ensemble set α1,2=(c1,2−1)\alpha_{1,2}=(c_{1,2}-1), with c2>1c_{2}>1, so that the cut [x−,x+][x_{-},x_{+}] is contained in the interval (0,1](0,1], see (5.8).

Theorem 7.3 (Covariances of Laguerre and Jacobi ensembles at leading order in nn).

Let XnX_{n} be in the Laguerre (resp. Jacobi) ensemble with c>1c>1 (resp. c2>1c_{2}>1). Denote the edges of the cut by 0<x−<x+0<x_{-}<x_{+}. Then, for all β>0\beta>0,

(7.9) limn→∞C−k,−l=(1x−​x+)k+l​limn→∞Ck,l.\lim_{n\to\infty}C_{-k,-l}=\left(\frac{1}{x_{-}x_{+}}\right)^{k+l}\lim_{n\to\infty}C_{k,l}.

More explicitly:

(7.10) limn→∞C−k,−l\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}C_{-k,-l} =(1c−1)2​(k+l)​limn→∞Ck,l\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{c-1}\right)^{2(k+l)}\lim_{n\to\infty}C_{k,l} (Laguerre)

Proof.

By the one-cut property, the limit

(7.12) G2,0​(z,w)=limn→∞G⁡(z,w),G_{2,0}(z,w)=\lim_{n\to\infty}G(z,w),

Using (7.7)-(7.8), the claim follows. ∎

8. Orthogonal and Symplectic ensembles

We will now discuss analogous results for the orthogonal and symplectic ensembles of random matrices, corresponding to averages over the density (3.1) with β=1\beta=1 or β=4\beta=4 respectively. Our aim will be to isolate the polynomial factors of the moments (Mellin transforms), again for the Gaussian, Laguerre and Jacobi ensembles. These ensembles are characterized by their joint eigenvalue distribution as in (3.1) with corresponding weight functions (3.2). We will consider various expectation values of power of traces with respect to (3.1) with β=1\beta=1 and 44. We will use the shorthand GSE and GOE to mean Gaussian Symplectic Ensemble, GSE (β=4\beta=4), Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble, GOE (β=1\beta=1) and similarly for the Laguerre (LSE / LOE) and Jacobi (JSE / JOE) cases. As in the complex case, we will denote by α=m−n\alpha=m-n in the Laguerre case, and α1=m1−n\alpha_{1}=m_{1}-n and α2=m2−n\alpha_{2}=m_{2}-n in the Jacobi case, which we treat as fixed nn-independent parameters.

Moments of real and quaternionic Gaussian ensembles have already received some attention in the literature, however much less is known compared with the complex case β=2\beta=2. One of the first explicit formulas was derived by Goulden and Jackson [40] who were motivated by the fact that, for β=1\beta=1, moments of Gaussian matrices describe the genus expansion of non-orientable surfaces. An important development was achieved in the work of Ledoux [53] who discovered recursion relations for moments of the GOE and GSE (which can be viewed as real and quaternionic analogues of the Harer-Zagier recurrence relations). This was extended to the Laguerre ensemble in [27]. Results holding for complex moments were obtained in [62] .

8.1. Recurrence relations and hypergeometric representations

We define

Qkℝ​(n)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(n) =𝔼​Tr⁡Xn2​k\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{2k} if Xn∼GOEX_{n}\sim\mathrm{GOE}
Qkℍ​(n)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n) =𝔼​Tr⁡Xn2​k\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{2k} if Xn∼GSEX_{n}\sim\mathrm{GSE}
Qkℝ​(m,n)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n) =𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k} if Xn∼LOEX_{n}\sim\mathrm{LOE}
Qkℍ​(m,n)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(m,n) =𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k} if Xn∼LSEX_{n}\sim\mathrm{LSE}
Qkℝ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k} if Xn∼JOEX_{n}\sim\mathrm{JOE}
Qkℍ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =𝔼​Tr⁡Xnk\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}X_{n}^{k} if Xn∼JSEX_{n}\sim\mathrm{JSE}
Δ​Qkℝ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =Qkℝ​(α1,α2,n)−Qk+1ℝ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle=Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)-Q_{k+1}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)
Δ​Qkℍ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =Qkℍ​(α1,α2,n)−Qk+1ℍ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle=Q_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)-Q_{k+1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)

for all k∈ℂk\in\mathbb{C} for which the expectations exist. Moments of the classical orthogonal ensembles satisfy recursions similar to those of the unitary ensembles. To our knowledge this was first noticed by Ledoux for the GOE [53] and extended to the LOE in [28]. The first question is whether moments of orthogonal / symplectic ensembles enjoy reflection symmetries and have orthogonal polynomial factors as in the unitary case. This is not the case as can be ascertained from the following observation. The Harer-Zagier recursion for moments ℚkℂ​(n)\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(n) of the GUE is a three terms recursion in kk which can be interpreted as the discrete S-L problem of some families of hypergeometric (Meixner / Meixner-Pollaczek) polynomials. Moments of the classical orthogonal ensembles satisfy recursion formulae too. For the GOE, Ledoux [53] discovered that Qkℝ​(n)Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(n) satisfy a five term recurrence relation which cannot be interpreted as a S-L equation (a second order difference equation). In fact, Ledoux also found an alternative inhomogeneous recursion formula for Qkℝ​(n)Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(n) coupled with the moments of the GUE that is somewhat more convenient for some application. An analogue of this coupled recursion was obtained later for the LOE [28].

These results suggest that suitable combinations of moments, rather than the moments themselves, have nice hypergeometric polynomial factors similar to the unitary cases.

Moments of the symplectic ensembles can be analysed similarly given the duality relations between moments of GSE, LSE and JSE of size nn and the (formal) moments of the GOE, LOE and JSE of size −2​n-2n

(8.1) Qkℍ​(n)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n) =(−1)k+1​2−1​Qkℝ​(−2​n)\displaystyle=(-1)^{k+1}2^{-1}Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(-2n)
(8.2) Qkℍ​(m,n)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(m,n) =(−1)k+1​2−1​Qkℝ​(−2​m,−2​n)\displaystyle=(-1)^{k+1}2^{-1}Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(-2m,-2n)
(8.3) Qkℍ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =−2−1​Qkℝ​(−2​α1,−2​α2,−2​n).\displaystyle=-2^{-1}Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(-2\alpha_{1},-2\alpha_{2},-2n).

For the GOE/GSE the duality was put forward by Mulase and Waldron in terms diagrammatic expansion of Gaussian integrals [66]. See also [53, 19]. This duality between orthogonal and symplectic Laguerre ensembles appeared in the paper of Hanlon, Stanley and Stembridge [45, Corollary 4.2]. The duality in the Jacobi ensembles has been observed by Forrester, Rahman and Witte [37, Eq. (4.15)]. See also [32] and  [38, Appendix B].

Theorem 8.1.

The combinations of GOE and GSE moments

(8.4) Skℝ​(n)\displaystyle S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(n) =Qk+1ℝ​(n)−(4​n−2)​Qkℝ​(n)−8​k​(2​k−1)​Qk−1ℝ​(n)\displaystyle=Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k+1}(n)-(4n-2)Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(n)-8k(2k-1)Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k-1}(n)
(8.5) Skℍ​(n)\displaystyle S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n) =2​Qk+1ℍ​(n)−(16​n+4)​Qkℍ​(n)−16​k​(2​k−1)​Qk−1ℍ​(n)\displaystyle=2Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k+1}(n)-(16n+4)Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(n)-16k(2k-1)Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k-1}(n)

have Meixner polynomial factors:

(8.6) Skℝ​(n)\displaystyle S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(n) =−3​n​(n−1)​(2​k−1)!!​Mn−2​(k,3,−1)\displaystyle=-3n(n-1)\;(2k-1)!!\;M_{n-2}(k;3,-1)
(8.7) =−3​n​(n−1)​(2​k−1)!!​Mk​(n−2,3,−1)\displaystyle=-3n(n-1)\;(2k-1)!!\;M_{k}(n-2;3,-1)
(8.8) Skℍ​(n)\displaystyle S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n) =−6​n​(2​n+1)​(2​k−1)!!​M2​n−1​(k,3,−1)\displaystyle=-6n(2n+1)\;(2k-1)!!\;M_{2n-1}(k;3,-1)
(8.9) =−6​n​(2​n+1)​(2​k−1)!!​Mk​(2​n−1,3,−1).\displaystyle=-6n(2n+1)\;(2k-1)!!\;M_{k}(2n-1;3,-1).

In particular, for any integer nn, Skℝ​(n)/(2​k−1)!!S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(n)/(2k-1)!! and Skℍ​(n)/(2​k−1)!!S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n)/(2k-1)!! are Meixner-Pollaczek polynomials in x=−i⁡(k+3/2)x=-i(k+3/2)

(8.10) Skℝ​(n)(2​k−1)!!\displaystyle\frac{S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(n)}{(2k-1)!!} =−6​in−2​Pn−2(3/2)​(x,π/2)\displaystyle=-6i^{n-2}\;P^{(3/2)}_{n-2}(x;\pi/2)
(8.11) Skℍ​(n)(2​k−1)!!\displaystyle\frac{S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n)}{(2k-1)!!} =−6​i2​n−1​P2​n−1(3/2)​(x,π/2)\displaystyle=-6i^{2n-1}\;P^{(3/2)}_{2n-1}(x;\pi/2)

invariant up to a change of sign under the reflection k→−3−kk\to-3-k, with complex zeros on the vertical line Re(k)=−3/2\operatorname{Re}(k)=-3/2.

Proof.

We first prove (8.6). We read from Ledoux paper [53, Theorem 3]

Skℝ​(n)=Qk+1ℂ​(n)−(4​n−3)​Qkℂ​(n)−2​k​(2​k−1)​Qk−1ℂ​(n).\displaystyle S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(n)=Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k+1}(n)-(4n-3)Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(n)-2k(2k-1)Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k-1}(n).

Using the polynomial property of Qkℂ​(n)Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(n), this remainder can be expressed as a sum of two Meixner polynomials

Skℝ​(n)=3​n​(2​k−1)!!​(Mn−1​(k,2,−1)−Mn−1​(k+1,2,−1))\displaystyle S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(n)=3n\;(2k-1)!!\;\left(M_{n-1}(k;2,-1)-M_{n-1}(k+1;2,-1)\right)

The representation (8.6) in terms of a single Meixner polynomial follows using the Forward Shift Operator [48, Eq. (9.10.6)].

To prove (8.8) the starting point is again a result in Ledoux paper [53, Theorem 5]

Skℍ​(n)=Qk+1ℝ​(2​n+1)−(8​n+2)​Qkℝ​(2​n+1)−8​k​(2​k−1)​Qk−1ℝ​(2​n+1),\displaystyle S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n)=Q_{k+1}^{\mathbb{R}}(2n+1)-(8n+2)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(2n+1)-8k(2k-1)Q_{k-1}^{\mathbb{R}}(2n+1),

which can be written in the insightful form

Skℍ​(n)=Skℝ​(2​n+1).\displaystyle S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n)=S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(2n+1).

The representation (8.8) is now a consequence of (8.6). Alternatively, by the duality relation (8.1)

Skℍ​(n)=(−1)k​(Qk+1ℝ​(−2​n)+(8​n+2)​Qkℝ​(−2​n)−8​k​(2​k−1)​Qk−1ℝ​(−2​n)),\displaystyle S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n)=(-1)^{k}\left(Q_{k+1}^{\mathbb{R}}(-2n)+(8n+2)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(-2n)-8k(2k-1)Q_{k-1}^{\mathbb{R}}(-2n)\right),

that is

Skℍ​(n)=(−1)k​Skℝ​(−2​n).\displaystyle S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n)=(-1)^{k}S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(-2n).

Using the self-duality of Meixner polynomials, we write

Skℍ​(n)=(−1)k+1​6​n​(2​n+1)​(2​k−1)!!​Mk​(−2​n−2,3,−1).\displaystyle S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n)=(-1)^{k+1}6n(2n+1)\;(2k-1)!!\;M_{k}(-2n-2;3,-1).

Now we use the symmetry (−1)k+1​Mk​(−2​n−2,3,−1)=Mk​(2​n+1,3,−1)(-1)^{k+1}M_{k}(-2n-2;3,-1)=M_{k}(2n+1;3,-1), and the self-duality again to conclude the proof. ∎

The S-L problem satisfied by the Meixner polynomials is a three term recursion formula for Skℝ​(n)S^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(n) and Skℍ​(n)S^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(n),

(8.12) (k+3)​Sk+1ℝ​(n)=(2​k+1)​(2​n−1)​Skℝ​(n)+k⁡(2​k+1)​(2​k−1)​Sk−1ℝ​(n)\displaystyle(k+3)S^{\mathbb{R}}_{k+1}(n)=(2k+1)(2n-1)S^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(n)+k(2k+1)(2k-1)S^{\mathbb{R}}_{k-1}(n)
(8.13) (k+3)​Sk+1ℍ​(n)=(2​k+1)​(4​n+1)​Skℍ​(n)+k⁡(2​k+1)​(2​k−1)​Sk−1ℍ​(n)\displaystyle(k+3)S^{\mathbb{H}}_{k+1}(n)=(2k+1)(4n+1)S^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(n)+k(2k+1)(2k-1)S^{\mathbb{H}}_{k-1}(n)

These recursions, which are very similar to the Harer-Zagier formula, become five term recurrences for the moments Qkℝ​(n)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(n) (this is Ledoux recursion [53, Theorem 2]) and Qkℍ​(n)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n).

Corollary 8.2.
(k+1)​Qkℝ​(n)\displaystyle(k+1)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(n) =(4​k−1)​(2​n−1)​Qk−1ℝ​(n)\displaystyle=(4k-1)(2n-1)Q_{k-1}^{\mathbb{R}}(n)
+(2​k−3)​(10​k2−9​k−8​n2+8​n)​Qk−2ℝ​(n)\displaystyle+(2k-3)(10k^{2}-9k-8n^{2}+8n)Q_{k-2}^{\mathbb{R}}(n)
−5​(2​k−3)​(2​k−4)​(2​k−5)​(2​n−1)​Qk−3ℝ​(n)\displaystyle-5(2k-3)(2k-4)(2k-5)(2n-1)Q_{k-3}^{\mathbb{R}}(n)
(8.14) −2​(2​k−3)​(2​k−4)​(2​k−5)​(2​k−6)​(2​k−7)​Qk−4ℝ​(n).\displaystyle-2(2k-3)(2k-4)(2k-5)(2k-6)(2k-7)Q_{k-4}^{\mathbb{R}}(n).
(k+1)​Qkℍ​(n)\displaystyle(k+1)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(n) =(4​k−1)​(4​n+1)​Qk−1ℍ​(n)\displaystyle=(4k-1)(4n+1)Q_{k-1}^{\mathbb{H}}(n)
+(2​k−3)​(10​k2−9​k−32​n2−16​n)​Qk−2ℍ​(n)\displaystyle+(2k-3)(10k^{2}-9k-32n^{2}-16n)Q_{k-2}^{\mathbb{H}}(n)
−5​(2​k−3)​(2​k−4)​(2​k−5)​(4​n+1)​Qk−3ℍ​(n)\displaystyle-5(2k-3)(2k-4)(2k-5)(4n+1)Q_{k-3}^{\mathbb{H}}(n)
(8.15) −2​(2​k−3)​(2​k−4)​(2​k−5)​(2​k−6)​(2​k−7)​Qk−4ℍ​(n).\displaystyle-2(2k-3)(2k-4)(2k-5)(2k-6)(2k-7)Q_{k-4}^{\mathbb{H}}(n).
Theorem 8.3.

Set α=m−n\alpha=m-n, and consider the following combinations of moments for the LOE and the LSE.

(8.16) Skℝ​(m,n)=Qk+1ℝ​(m,n)−2​(m+n−1)​Qkℝ​(m,n)−(1−α2+4​k​(k−1))​Qk−1ℝ​(m,n)S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n)=Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k+1}(m,n)-2(m+n-1)Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(m,n)\\ -(1-\alpha^{2}+4k(k-1))Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k-1}(m,n)
(8.17) Skℍ​(m,n)=2​Qk+1ℍ​(m,n)−(8​m+8​n+4)​Qkℍ​(m,n)−(2−8​α2+8​k​(k−1))​Qk−1ℍ​(m,n)S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(m,n)=2Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k+1}(m,n)-(8m+8n+4)Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(m,n)\\ -(2-8\alpha^{2}+8k(k-1))Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k-1}(m,n)

Then, Skℝ​(m,n𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n and Skℍ​(m,n)S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(m,n) can be written in terms of dual Hahn polynomials (as functions of kk) or Hahn polynomials (as functions of nn):

(8.18) Skℝ​(m,n)(k+α)!\displaystyle\frac{S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n)}{(k+\alpha)!} =−6(n−2)!​(m−2)!​Sn−2​(x2,52,12,α+12)\displaystyle=-\frac{6}{(n-2)!(m-2)!}\;S_{n-2}\left(x^{2};\;\frac{5}{2},\frac{1}{2},\alpha+\frac{1}{2}\right)
(8.19) =−3​n​m​(n−1)​(m−1)(α+2)!​Qk−2​(n−2, 2,2,−3−α)\displaystyle=-\frac{3nm(n-1)(m-1)}{(\alpha+2)!}\;Q_{k-2}(n-2;\;2,2,-3-\alpha)
(8.20) Skℍ​(m,n)(k+2​α)!\displaystyle\frac{S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(m,n)}{(k+2\alpha)!} =−24​n​m(2​n)!​(2​m)!​S2​n−1​(x2,52,12,2​α+12)\displaystyle=-\frac{24nm}{(2n)!(2m)!}\;S_{2n-1}\left(x^{2},\frac{5}{2},\frac{1}{2},2\alpha+\frac{1}{2}\right)
(8.21) =−12​n​m​(2​n+1)​(2​m+1)(2​α+2)!​Qk−2​(2​n−1, 2,2,−3−2​α)\displaystyle=-\frac{12nm(2n+1)(2m+1)}{(2\alpha+2)!}\;Q_{k-2}(2n-1;\,2,2,-3-2\alpha)

where k=i​x−1/2k=ix-1/2. In particular this shows that the polynomials Skℝ​(m,n)/(k+α)!S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n)/(k+\alpha)! and Skℍ​(m,n)/(k+2​α)!S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(m,n)/(k+2\alpha)! are invariant under the reflection k→−1−kk\to-1-k (reciprocity law) and, moreover, their zeros lie on the critical line Re(k)=−1/2\operatorname{Re}(k)=-1/2.

Proof.

By the inhomogeneous recursion for moments of the LOE [28, Theorem 3.5], Skℝ​(m,n)S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n) is a combination of moments of the LUE

Skℝ​(m,n)=3k−1​((m+n−k−1)​Qkℂ​(m−1,n−1)−Qk+1ℂ​(m−1,n−1)),\displaystyle S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n)=\frac{3}{k-1}((m+n-k-1)Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(m-1,n-1)-Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k+1}(m-1,n-1)),

that can be expressed in terms of continuous dual Hahn polynomials

Skℝ(m,n)=3​(k+α)!(k−1)​(m−2)!​(n−2)!×((m+n−k−1)​Sn−2​(x2,32,12,α+12)−(m−n+k+1)​Sn−2​((x−i)2,32,12,α+12))S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n)=\frac{3(k+\alpha)!}{(k-1)(m-2)!(n-2)!}\times\\ \biggl((m+n-k-1)S_{n-2}\left(x^{2};\;\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2},\alpha+\frac{1}{2}\right)-(m-n+k+1)S_{n-2}\left((x-i)^{2};\;\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2},\alpha+\frac{1}{2}\right)\biggr)

The final result (8.18) can be obtained by using the Forward Shift Operator of the continuous dual Hahn polynomials [48, Eq. (9.3.7)]. From the hypergeometric representation of Hahn polynomials we get (8.19).

For the symplectic moments, note that, by duality (8.2) between LOE and LSE moments,

Skℍ​(m,n)=(−1)k​Skℝ​(−2​m,−2​n).S_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(m,n)=(-1)^{k}S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(-2m,-2n).

This proves (8.21). We use the identity (3−2​α)k−2​Qk−2​(−2​n−2, 2,2,−3+2​α)=(−1)k​(3+2​α)k−2​Qk−2​(2​n−1, 2,2,−3−2​α)(3-2\alpha)_{k-2}Q_{k-2}(-2n-2;\;2,2,-3+2\alpha)=(-1)^{k}(3+2\alpha)_{k-2}Q_{k-2}(2n-1;\;2,2,-3-2\alpha) and find (8.21). Now, this can be written as a polynomial in kk which can be cast as (8.20). ∎

Remark.

As in the Gaussian case, there is a reflection formula under the transformation 2​m+1→−2​m2m+1\to-2m and 2​n+1→−2​n2n+1\to-2n

(8.22) Sℝ​(2​m+1,2​n+1)=(−1)k​Sℝ​(−2​m,−2​n).S^{\mathbb{R}}(2m+1,2n+1)=(-1)^{k}S^{\mathbb{R}}(-2m,-2n).

The S-L problem of continuous dual Hahn polynomials corresponds to the three term recursions (in kk)

(8.23) (k+3)​Sk+1ℝ​(m,n)\displaystyle(k+3)S^{\mathbb{R}}_{k+1}(m,n) =(2​k+1)​(2​n+α−1)​Skℝ​(m,n)+(k−2)​(k2−α2)​Sk−1ℝ​(m,n)\displaystyle=(2k+1)(2n+\alpha-1)S^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(m,n)+(k-2)(k^{2}-\alpha^{2})S^{\mathbb{R}}_{k-1}(m,n)
(8.24) (k+3)​Sk+1ℍ​(m,n)\displaystyle(k+3)S^{\mathbb{H}}_{k+1}(m,n) =(2​k+1)​(4​n+2​α+1)​Skℍ​(m,n)+(k−2)​(k2−4​α2)​Sk−1ℍ​(m,n)\displaystyle=(2k+1)(4n+2\alpha+1)S^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(m,n)+(k-2)(k^{2}-4\alpha^{2})S^{\mathbb{H}}_{k-1}(m,n)

which are similar to the Haagerup-Thorbjørnsen formula for the moments of the LUE. Writing Skℝ​(m,n)S^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(m,n) and Skℍ​(m,n)S^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(m,n) in terms of the moments we obtain the following five term recursions. To our knowledge these recursion formulae are new.

Corollary 8.4.
(8.25) (k+1)​Qkℝ​(m,n)\displaystyle(k+1)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n) =A​Qk−1ℝ​(m,n)+B​Qk−2ℝ​(m,n)+C​Qk−3ℝ​(m,n)+D​Qk−4ℝ​(m,n).\displaystyle=AQ_{k-1}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n)+BQ_{k-2}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n)+CQ_{k-3}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n)+DQ_{k-4}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n).

with

A\displaystyle A =(4​k−1)​(m+n−1)\displaystyle=(4k-1)(m+n-1)
B\displaystyle B =−(4​k−6)​(m+n−1)2+(k−4)​((k−2)2−α2)+(k+1)​((2​k−3)2−α2)\displaystyle=-(4k-6)(m+n-1)^{2}+(k-4)\left((k-2)^{2}-\alpha^{2}\right)+(k+1)\left((2k-3)^{2}-\alpha^{2}\right)
C\displaystyle C =−(m+n−1)​((2​k−3)​((2​k−5)2−α2)−(2​k−8)​((k−2)2−α2))\displaystyle=-(m+n-1)\left((2k-3)\left((2k-5)^{2}-\alpha^{2}\right)-(2k-8)\left((k-2)^{2}-\alpha^{2}\right)\right)
D\displaystyle D =−(k−4)​((k−2)2−α2)​((2​k−7)2−α2).\displaystyle=-(k-4)\left((k-2)^{2}-\alpha^{2}\right)\left((2k-7)^{2}-\alpha^{2}\right).

and

(8.26) (k+1)​Qkℍ​(m,n)\displaystyle(k+1)Q_{k}^{\mathbb{H}}(m,n) =A​Qk−1ℍ​(m,n)+B​Qk−2ℍ​(m,n)+C​Qk−3ℍ​(m,n)+D​Qk−4ℍ​(m,n).\displaystyle=AQ_{k-1}^{\mathbb{H}}(m,n)+BQ_{k-2}^{\mathbb{H}}(m,n)+CQ_{k-3}^{\mathbb{H}}(m,n)+DQ_{k-4}^{\mathbb{H}}(m,n).

with

A\displaystyle A =(4​k−1)​(2​m+2​n+1)\displaystyle=(4k-1)(2m+2n+1)
B\displaystyle B =−(4​k−6)​(2​m+2​n+1)2+(k−4)​((k−2)2−4​α2)+(k+1)​((2​k−3)2−4​α2)\displaystyle=-(4k-6)(2m+2n+1)^{2}+(k-4)\left((k-2)^{2}-4\alpha^{2}\right)+(k+1)\left((2k-3)^{2}-4\alpha^{2}\right)
C\displaystyle C =−(2​m+2​n+1)​((2​k−3)​((2​k−5)2−4​α2)−(2​k−8)​((k−2)2−4​α2))\displaystyle=-(2m+2n+1)\left((2k-3)\left((2k-5)^{2}-4\alpha^{2}\right)-(2k-8)\left((k-2)^{2}-4\alpha^{2}\right)\right)
D\displaystyle D =−(k−4)​((k−2)2−4​α2)​((2​k−7)2−4​α2).\displaystyle=-(k-4)\left((k-2)^{2}-4\alpha^{2}\right)\left((2k-7)^{2}-4\alpha^{2}\right).

Using methods similar to those in [28] it is possible to write a recursion formula for the moments of the JOE. Denote

Skℝ​(α1,α2,n)=(2​k+4−α1−α2−2​n)​(α1+α2+2​(n+k+1))​Δ​Qk+1ℝ​(α1,α2,n)+2​(α1​α2−α1−α2+α22−4​k​(1+k)−2​n+2​(α1+α2)​n+2​n2)​Δ​Qkℝ​(α1,α2,n)−(α22−(1−2​k)2)​Δ​Qk−1ℝ​(α1,α2,n).S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)=(2k+4-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}-2n)(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2(n+k+1))\Delta Q_{k+1}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)\\ +2(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{2}^{2}-4k(1+k)-2n+2(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})n+2n^{2})\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)\\ -(\alpha_{2}^{2}-(1-2k)^{2})\Delta Q_{k-1}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n).
Proposition 8.5 (Recursion for moments of the JOE).

Set α1=m1−n\alpha_{1}=m_{1}-n and α2=m2−n\alpha_{2}=m_{2}-n. Then the differences of adjacent moments Δ​Qkℝ​(α1,α2,n)\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) of the JOE satisfy the following inhomogeneous three term recursion

(8.27) Skℝ​(α1,α2,n)=3k−1​(((α1+α2)​(α2−k−1)+2​(α1+α2−k−1)​n+2​n2)​Δ​Qkℂ​(α1,α2,n−1)CLOSEOPEN−(α1+α2+2​n)​(α1+α2+2​n−k−3)​Δ​Qk+1ℂ​(α1,α2,n−1)),S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)=\\ \frac{3}{k-1}\Bigl(\left((\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})(\alpha_{2}-k-1)+2(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}-k-1)n+2n^{2}\right)\Delta Q_{k}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n-1)\\ -(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n)(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n-k-3)\Delta Q_{k+1}^{\mathbb{C}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n-1)\Bigr),

As in the Gaussian and Laguerre cases, the above recursion formula suggests that Skℝ​(α1,α2,n)S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n), and not the moments themselves, have a nice polynomial property. This is the content of the next theorem whose proof goes along the same lines as the Gaussian and Laguerre cases.

Theorem 8.6.

Set k=i​x−1/2k=ix-1/2. The combination Skℝ​(α1,α2,n)S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) has a Wilson polynomial factor

(8.28) Skℝ​(α1,α2,n)=(−1)n−1​6(n−2)!​(α1+n)​(α1+n−1)​(α1+α2+n)!(α2+n−2)!×(α2+k)!(α1+α2+k+2​n−1)!​Wn−2​(x2,52,12,α2+12,32−α1−α2−2​n).S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)=(-1)^{n-1}\frac{6}{(n-2)!}\frac{(\alpha_{1}+n)(\alpha_{1}+n-1)(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+n)!}{(\alpha_{2}+n-2)!}\\ \times\frac{(\alpha_{2}+k)!}{(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+k+2n-1)!}W_{n-2}\left(x^{2};\;\frac{5}{2},\frac{1}{2},\alpha_{2}+\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}-2n\right).

In particular, Skℝ​(α1,α2,n)​((α1+α2+k+2​n−1)!/(α2+k)!)S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)((\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+k+2n-1)!/(\alpha_{2}+k)!) is a polynomial of degree 2​(n−2)2(n-2) in kk, invariant under the reflection k→−1−kk\to-1-k, with zeros on the vertical line Re(k)=−1/2\operatorname{Re}(k)=-1/2.

8.2. Symplectic Ensembles

The goal of this section is to establish the following polynomial property for the moments of the symplectic ensembles.

Theorem 8.7.

The rescaled moments

(8.29) pnℍ​(k)={cn​1Γ⁡(k+1/2)​Qkℍ​(n)GSEcn,m​2kΓ⁡(2​α+k+2)​Qkℍ​(m,n)LSEcn,α1,α2​Γ⁡(1+2​α1+2​α2+4​n+k)Γ⁡(2​α1+k+2)​Δ​Qkℍ​(α1,α2,n)JSEp^{\mathbb{H}}_{n}(k)=\begin{cases}c_{n}\dfrac{1}{\Gamma(k+1/2)}Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(n)&\mathrm{GSE}\\ \\ c_{n,m}\dfrac{2^{k}}{\Gamma(2\alpha+k+2)}Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(m,n)&\mathrm{LSE}\\ \\ c_{n,\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}}\dfrac{\Gamma(1+2\alpha_{1}+2\alpha_{2}+4n+k)}{\Gamma(2\alpha_{1}+k+2)}\Delta Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)&\mathrm{JSE}\end{cases}

are monic polynomials in kk of degree 2​(n−1)2(n-1) in the GSE, and degree 4​(n−1)4(n-1) in the LSE and JSE cases. The normalizing constants are

{cn=22​(1−n)​Γ​(2​n)​πcn,m=Γ⁡(2​m)​Γ​(2​n)cn,α1,α2=Γ⁡(2​n+2​α1)​Γ​(2​α2+4)​Γ​(2​n)Γ⁡(2​α1+2​α2+2​n+2)​Γ​(2​α2+2​n+2)​(2​α2+2).\begin{cases}c_{n}=2^{2(1-n)}\Gamma(2n)\sqrt{\pi}\\ c_{n,m}=\Gamma(2m)\Gamma(2n)\\ c_{n,\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}}=\dfrac{\Gamma(2n+2\alpha_{1})\Gamma(2\alpha_{2}+4)\Gamma(2n)}{\Gamma(2\alpha_{1}+2\alpha_{2}+2n+2)\Gamma(2\alpha_{2}+2n+2)(2\alpha_{2}+2)}.\end{cases}
Proof.

We will discuss the Gaussian case in detail, as the Laguerre and Jacobi cases follow a similar pattern. By [62, Eq. (33)], we have the explicit formula

(8.30) Qkℍ​(n)=2−k−1​Qkℂ​(2​n)−an​∑j=1n∑i=0n−j(ki)​(ki+j)​(n−i−j+1)(k−1/2)Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(n)=2^{-k-1}Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(2n)-a_{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-j}{k\choose i}{k\choose i+j}(n-i-j+1)_{(k-1/2)}

where Qkℂ​(2​n)Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(2n) denotes the moments of the GUE (see Section 4.1) and

an=Γ⁡(n+1)​Γ​(n)π​Γ​(2​n)​41−n.a_{n}=\frac{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(n)}{\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(2n)4^{1-n}}.

Although formula (8.30) was only stated in [62] for k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, it naturally defines a meromorphic continuation to k∈ℂk\in\mathbb{C}, as follows. As a function of k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, we have that Q2​kℂ​(2​n)/(Γ⁡(k+1/2))Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{2k}(2n)/(\Gamma(k+1/2)) is a polynomial of degree 2​n−12n-1 in kk (see equation (4.4)) and hence is defined for any k∈ℂk\in\mathbb{C}. It remains to study the second term in (8.30). Note that

(n−i−j+1)(k−1/2)Γ⁡(k+1/2)\frac{(n-i-j+1)_{(k-1/2)}}{\Gamma(k+1/2)}

is a polynomial of degree n−i−jn-i-j, while (ki){k\choose i} and (ki+j){k\choose i+j} are polynomials of degree ii and i+ji+j respectively. Hence Qkℍ​(n)/Γ⁡(k+1/2)Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(n)/\Gamma(k+1/2) is a finite sum of polynomials in kk and is therefore a polynomial. To compute degrees, notice that the highest degree term in the summand of (8.30) occurs when 2​i+j+n−i−j=n+i2i+j+n-i-j=n+i is maximal, namely when i=n−1i=n-1 implying a degree of 2​n−12n-1. That the degree of the combined polynomials (i.e. unitary plus symplectic contribution) is really 2​n−22n-2 is a consequence of the following cancellation. Setting j=1j=1 and i=n−1i=n-1 in the summand of (8.30) and dividing by Γ⁡(k+1/2)\Gamma(k+1/2) gives the polynomial

an​(kn−1)​(kn)a_{n}{k\choose n-1}{k\choose n}

Then Stirling’s formula gives the estimate

an​(kn−1)​(kn)=k2​n−1(2​n−1)!​41−n+O⁡(k2​n−2),k→∞a_{n}{k\choose n-1}{k\choose n}=\frac{k^{2n-1}}{(2n-1)!4^{1-n}}+O(k^{2n-2}),\qquad k\to\infty

Similarly, consider the complex moments

12​Γ​(k+1/2)​Qkℂ​(2​n)=1π​∑j=02​n−12j−1​(kj)​(2​nj+1)\frac{1}{2\;\Gamma(k+1/2)}Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(2n)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\sum_{j=0}^{2n-1}2^{j-1}{k\choose j}{2n\choose j+1}

which has the same leading coefficient (setting j=2​n−1j=2n-1) as

1π​(k2​n−1)​22​n−2=k2​n−1​4n−1(2​n−1)!+O⁡(k2​n−2),k→∞\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}{k\choose 2n-1}2^{2n-2}=\frac{k^{2n-1}4^{n-1}}{(2n-1)!}+O(k^{2n-2}),\qquad k\to\infty

Hence the terms of order k2​n−1k^{2n-1} in (8.30) cancel, yielding a polynomial of degree 2​n−22n-2. To compute the normalizing factor cnc_{n} requires studying terms of order k2​n−2k^{2n-2}. This is a straightforward but tedious task and we omit the details. The only contributions to the monomial k2​n−2k^{2n-2} come from (8.2) when j=2​n−1j=2n-1 and j=2​n−2j=2n-2, and from the double sum in (8.30) with indices (i,j)=(n−1,1)(i,j)=(n-1,1) and (i,j)=(n−2,1),(n−2,2)(i,j)=(n-2,1),(n-2,2). Then studying the asymptotics of these five terms as k→∞k\to\infty with Stirling’s formula gives the result. For the Laguerre and Jacobi cases, this computation can be repeated with the formulae [62, Eq. (89) and Eq. (98)] which have an identical structure to (8.30) and is therefore omitted. ∎

Below are the first few polynomials pnℍ​(k)p^{\mathbb{H}}_{n}(k) for the GSE, whose zeros appear to settle onto an explicit contour in the complex plane as nn becomes larger (see Fig. 4).

p1ℍ​(k)=1p2ℍ​(k)=k2+5​k+3p3ℍ​(k)=k4+10​k3+38​k2+41​k+452p4ℍ​(k)=k6+15​k5+109​k4+393​k3+637​k2+735​k+315.\begin{split}p^{\mathbb{H}}_{1}(k)&=1\\ p^{\mathbb{H}}_{2}(k)&=k^{2}+5k+3\\ p^{\mathbb{H}}_{3}(k)&=k^{4}+10k^{3}+38k^{2}+41k+\frac{45}{2}\\ p^{\mathbb{H}}_{4}(k)&=k^{6}+15k^{5}+109k^{4}+393k^{3}+637k^{2}+735k+315.\end{split}

8.3. Orthogonal Ensembles

In this section we will study the Mellin transform of the one-point correlation function ρn(β)​(x)\rho_{n}^{(\beta)}(x) with β=1\beta=1. One can expect this case to be more complicated in general, since now (3.1) contains a non-analytic term (the absolute value of the Vandermonde determinant, which happened to be a polynomial in the cases β=2\beta=2 and β=4\beta=4). In the case of nn odd we are saved by a remarkable duality principle for the Mellin transform, relating the orthogonal and symplectic ensembles. This duality involves a simple correction term which is a single hypergeometric OP.

The case of nn even has a different analytic structure, evident already at n=2n=2. Indeed, it was known since the beginnings of random matrix theory that the parity nn plays an important role for ensembles with orthogonal symmetry (see [58, Chapter 6] for example or more recently [35]), with most authors assuming nn to be even for simplicity. Here it is the converse, we describe the analytic structure for nn odd and give an explicit analytic continuation. First we need a proposition relating the orthogonal and symplectic ensembles.

Proposition 8.8.

Given the notation of Section 3, let pn​(x)p_{n}(x) denote the degree nn monic polynomial orthogonal with respect to the weight w2​(x)w_{2}(x) on the interval II. Then the one-point eigenvalue density (3.3) satisfies the following duality

(8.31) ρ2​n+1(1)​(x)=2​ρ~n(4)​(x)+w1​(x)​p2​n​(x)∫Iw1​(t)​p2​n​(t)​𝑑t\rho^{(1)}_{2n+1}(x)=2\tilde{\rho}^{(4)}_{n}(x)+\frac{w_{1}(x)p_{2n}(x)}{\int_{I}w_{1}(t)p_{2n}(t)\,dt}

where ρ~(4)​(x)\tilde{\rho}^{(4)}(x) is the β=4\beta=4 eigenvalue density with respect to the modified weights

(8.32) w~4​(x)={e−x2/2Hermitexα+1​e−xLaguerrexα1+1​(1−x)α2+1Jacobi.\tilde{w}_{4}(x)=\begin{cases}e^{-x^{2}/2}&\text{Hermite}\\ x^{\alpha+1}e^{-x}&\text{Laguerre}\\ x^{\alpha_{1}+1}(1-x)^{\alpha_{2}+1}&\text{Jacobi}.\end{cases}
Remark.

We give a complete proof of Propostition 8.8 in Appendix A, which is based on the skew-orthogonal polynomial formalism developed in [3]. In the specific case of the GOE, formula (8.31) was mentioned in [53]. Actually, the statement of Proposition 8.8 is implicit in Forrester’s book [36, (6.120)-(6.122)]. It is worth emphasizing that this duality goes beyond the one-point function and can be formulated as a duality between the correlation kernels of nn-odd orthogonal and symplectic ensembles. This suggests a possibly simpler route to studying correlation functions of nn-odd orthogonal ensembles, but this lies beyond the scope of the current investigation.

We now study the consequences of the duality (8.31) for the Mellin transforms of the orthogonal ensembles.

Theorem 8.9 (Duality in the nn-odd orthogonal ensemble).

In the three orthogonal ensembles the following identity holds for all k∈ℂk\in\mathbb{C} and n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}:

(8.33) Qkℝ​(2​n+1)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(2n+1) =2k+1​Qkℍ​(n)+4k​Γ​(k+1/2)​fk​(n)\displaystyle=2^{k+1}Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(n)+4^{k}\Gamma\left(k+1/2\right)f_{k}(n)
(8.34) Qkℝ​(2​m+1,2​n+1)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(2m+1,2n+1) =2k+1​Qkℍ​(m,n)+2k​Γ​(k+m−n+1/2)​fk​(m,n)\displaystyle=2^{k+1}Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}\left(m,n\right)+2^{k}\Gamma\left(k+m-n+1/2\right)f_{k}(m,n)
(8.35) Qkℝ​(2​α1,2​α2,2​n+1)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(2\alpha_{1},2\alpha_{2},2n+1) =2​Qkℍ​(α1,α2,n)+Γ⁡(k+α1+1/2)Γ⁡(k+α1+α2+2​n+1)​fk​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle=2Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}\left(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n\right)+\dfrac{\Gamma\left(k+\alpha_{1}+1/2\right)}{\Gamma\left(k+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n+1\right)}f_{k}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)\

where

{fk​(n)=cn​Pn(1/4)​(−i⁡(k+1/4),π/2)fk​(m,n)=cn,m​P2​n(m−n+1/2)​(−i​k,π/2)fk​(α1,α2,n)=cn,α1,α2​p2​n​(−i​k,α1+12,−α1−α2−2​n,α1+12,−α1−α2−2​n).\begin{cases}f_{k}(n)=c_{n}P^{(1/4)}_{n}(-i(k+1/4);\pi/2)\\ \\ f_{k}(m,n)=c_{n,m}P^{(m-n+1/2)}_{2n}(-ik;\pi/2)\\ \\ f_{k}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n)=c_{n,\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}}p_{2n}(-ik;\alpha_{1}+\frac{1}{2},-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}-2n,\alpha_{1}+\frac{1}{2},-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}-2n).\end{cases}

In each case, the fkf_{k} is a hypergeometric orthogonal polynomial from the Askey scheme: The Pn(λ)​(x,ϕ)P^{(\lambda)}_{n}(x,\phi) are the Meixner-Pollaczek polynomials, while pn​(x,a,b,c,d)p_{n}(x;a,b,c,d) are the continuous Hahn polynomials, see (3.14). The normalization constants are

{cn=in​n!Γ⁡(n+1/2)cn,m=(−1)n​n!Γ⁡(m+1/2)cn,α1,α2=(−1)n​n!​Γ​(α1+1/2)​Γ​(n+α1+α2+1)Γ⁡(n+α1+1/2)​Γ​(n+α2+1/2).\begin{cases}c_{n}=\dfrac{i^{n}n!}{\Gamma\left(n+1/2\right)}\\ c_{n,m}=\dfrac{(-1)^{n}n!}{\Gamma\left(m+1/2\right)}\\ c_{n,\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}}=\dfrac{(-1)^{n}n!\Gamma\left(\alpha_{1}+1/2\right)\Gamma\left(n+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+1\right)}{\Gamma\left(n+\alpha_{1}+1/2\right)\Gamma\left(n+\alpha_{2}+1/2\right)}.\end{cases}
Remark.

The results (8.33)-(8.35) combined with Theorem 8.7 imply a polynomial property for the moments of the orthogonal ensemble, though not as cleanly as in the symplectic case. It is not possible to normalize Qkℝ​(2​n+1)Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(2n+1) and obtain a polynomial in kk, unlike in the symplectic and unitary cases (e.g. the second term in (8.33) is always exponentially larger in kk than the first).

The content of Theorems 8.1 and 8.3 is that the combinations Skℝ​(n)S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(n) and Skℝ​(m,n)S_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n) of moments of the orthogonal ensembles (with fixed nn) have hypergeometric orthogonal polynomial factors. Putting together the dualities in the nn-odd orthogonal ensembles of Theorem 8.9 and the classical duality between symplectic moments and formal orthogonal moments (8.1)-(8.2)-(8.3), we find that the combinations of moments (with fixed kk)

Tkℝ​(n)\displaystyle T_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(n) =Qkℝ​(2​n+1)+(−2)k​Qkℝ​(−2​n)\displaystyle=Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(2n+1)+(-2)^{k}Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(-2n)
Tkℝ​(m,n)\displaystyle T_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n) =Qkℝ​(2​m+1,2​n+1)+(−2)k​Qkℝ​(−2​m,−2​n)\displaystyle=Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(2m+1,2n+1)+(-2)^{k}Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(-2m,-2n)
Tkℝ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle T_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =Qkℝ​(2​α1,2​α2,2​n+1)+Qkℝ​(−2​α1,−2​α2,−2​n)\displaystyle=Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(2\alpha_{1},2\alpha_{2},2n+1)+Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(-2\alpha_{1},-2\alpha_{2},-2n)

do have hypergeometric polynomial factors.

Corollary 8.10.
(8.36) Tkℝ​(n)\displaystyle T_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(n) =(2​k−1)!!​Mn​(k, 1/2,−1)\displaystyle=(2k-1)!!\;M_{n}\left(k;\;1/2,-1\right)
(8.37) Tkℝ​(m,n)\displaystyle T_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(m,n) =2m+n+kπ​Γ⁡(k+α+1/2)(2​n−1)!!​(2​m−1)!!​Sn​((i​k)2, 1/2,0,α+1/2)\displaystyle=\frac{2^{m+n+k}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\frac{\Gamma(k+\alpha+1/2)}{(2n-1)!!(2m-1)!!}\;S_{n}((ik)^{2};\;1/2,0,\alpha+1/2)
Tkℝ​(α1,α2,n)\displaystyle T_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},n) =Γ⁡(k+α1+1/2)​Γ​(α1+1/2)​Γ​(n+α1+α2+1)Γ⁡(k+α1+α2+2​n+1)​Γ​(n+α1+1/2)​Γ​(n+α2+1/2)\displaystyle=\dfrac{\Gamma\left(k+\alpha_{1}+1/2\right)\Gamma\left(\alpha_{1}+1/2\right)\Gamma\left(n+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+1\right)}{\Gamma\left(k+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2n+1\right)\Gamma\left(n+\alpha_{1}+1/2\right)\Gamma\left(n+\alpha_{2}+1/2\right)}
(8.38) (2​(n+α2)−1)!!(2​α2−1)!!​(2​n−1)!!​(−1)n​Wn​((i​k)2,12,0,α1+12,−α1−α2−2​n).\displaystyle\frac{(2(n+\alpha_{2})-1)!!}{(2\alpha_{2}-1)!!(2n-1)!!}(-1)^{n}W_{n}\left((ik)^{2};\;\frac{1}{2},0,\alpha_{1}+\frac{1}{2},-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}-2n\right).
Proof of Theorem 8.9.

We multiply both sides of identity (8.31) by xkx^{k} (or |x|2​k|x|^{2k} for the GOE) and integrate over II. By the correspondence (3.4) this gives

(8.39) Qkℝ​(2​n+1)=2​Q~kℍ​(n)+ψn​(k)Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(2n+1)=2\tilde{Q}^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(n)+\psi_{n}(k)

where Q~kℍ​(n)\tilde{Q}^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(n) are moments defined with respect to the modified weights (8.32). Such moments are easily expressed in terms of the usual Qkℍ​(n)Q^{\mathbb{H}}_{k}(n) by multiplying by 2k2^{k} (Hermite and Laguerre case) or by dividing the parameters α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} by 22 (Laguerre and Jacobi cases). This gives the first terms in (8.33)-(8.35).

The correction ψn​(k)\psi_{n}(k) is a weighted Mellin transform of the corresponding orthogonal polynomial. In the JOE and LOE this takes the form

(8.40) ψn​(k)=∫Ixk​w1​(x)​p2​n​(x)​𝑑x∫Iw1​(x)​p2​n​(x)​𝑑x.\psi_{n}(k)=\frac{\int_{I}x^{k}w_{1}(x)p_{2n}(x)\,dx}{\int_{I}w_{1}(x)p_{2n}(x)\,dx}.

while for the GOE xkx^{k} is replaced with |x|2​k|x|^{2k}. The integral (8.40) can be computed explicitly by expanding p2​n​(x)p_{2n}(x) as a sum and integrating term by term. This expansion turns out to be a terminating hypergeometric series which can be identified as one of the hypergeometric polynomials appearing in the claimed result. In fact, for the Gaussian and Laguerre cases, precisely this calculation is carried out in a different context in [23], so let us just explain the Jacobi case. Then the monic polynomials p2​n​(x)p_{2n}(x) are proportional to the usual Jacobi polynomials which can be written down explicitly (see e.g. [73, Eq. 4.32]). Integrating term by term in (8.40) gives

ψn​(k)=n!​Γ​(α1+α22+1+n)Γ⁡(α1+12+n)​Γ​(α2+12+n)​Γ​(α1+α22+2​n+k+1)×∑i=02​n(−1)i​(2​n+α22​n−i)​(2​n+α1i)​Γ​(α2+12+i+k)​Γ​(α1+12+2​n−i).\begin{split}&\psi_{n}(k)=\frac{n!\Gamma(\frac{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}{2}+1+n)}{\Gamma(\frac{\alpha_{1}+1}{2}+n)\Gamma(\frac{\alpha_{2}+1}{2}+n)\Gamma(\frac{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}{2}+2n+k+1)}\\ &\times\sum_{i=0}^{2n}(-1)^{i}\binom{2n+\alpha_{2}}{2n-i}\binom{2n+\alpha_{1}}{i}\Gamma\left(\frac{\alpha_{2}+1}{2}+i+k\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{\alpha_{1}+1}{2}+2n-i\right).\end{split}

The sum can be matched with a hypergeometric function and we obtain

ψn​(k)=ηn,α1,α2​Γ​(α2+12+k)Γ⁡(1+α1+α22+k+2​n)​F23​(k+(α2+1)/2,−2​n,−α1−2​nα2+1,−(α1−1)/2−2n,1)\psi_{n}(k)=\frac{\eta_{n,\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}}\Gamma\left(\frac{\alpha_{2}+1}{2}+k\right)}{\Gamma\left(1+\frac{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}{2}+k+2n\right)}\,{}_{3}F_{2}\left(\begin{matrix}k+(\alpha_{2}+1)/2,-2n,-\alpha_{1}-2n\\ \alpha_{2}+1,-(\alpha_{1}-1)/2-2n\end{matrix};1\right)

where

ηn,α1,α2=n!​Γ​(1+α1+α22+n)​Γ​(1+α2+2​n)​Γ​(1+α12+2​n)(2​n)!​Γ​(1+α2)​Γ​(1+α12+n)​Γ​(1+α22+n).\eta_{n,\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}}=\frac{n!\Gamma(1+\frac{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}{2}+n)\Gamma(1+\alpha_{2}+2n)\Gamma(\frac{1+\alpha_{1}}{2}+2n)}{(2n)!\Gamma(1+\alpha_{2})\Gamma(\frac{1+\alpha_{1}}{2}+n)\Gamma(\frac{1+\alpha_{2}}{2}+n)}.

Finally, comparing (8.3) with the definition of the continuous Hahn polynomial in (3.14) gives the result. ∎

Remark.

In the Gaussian and Laguerre cases, the evaluation of the integral (8.40) already appeared in the literature on special functions, see the work of Bump et al. [21], Coffey et al.[23, 24], though no connection to random matrix theory is made. These works show that the quantity (8.40) satisfies a functional equation and Riemann hypothesis with critical line Re(k)=−1/2\mathrm{Re}(k)=-1/2 (Hermite polynomials) and Re⁡(k)=0\mathrm{Re}(k)=0 (Laguerre polynomials) in our notation. We believe it is new that precisely these Mellin transforms should appear in the context of random matrices. The last and most complicated case of Jacobi appears to be absent from the literature. This turns out to be a continuous Hahn polynomial p2​n​(−i​k,a,b,c,d)p_{2n}(-ik;a,b,c,d) with a=c>0a=c>0 and b=d<0b=d<0. The analogous properties in this case are most easily proved by noticing that the continuous Hahn polynomial can be represented in terms of the Wilson polynomial with a negative fourth parameter. Explicitly, one has

p2​n​(−i​k,α1+1/2,−α1−α2−2​n,α1+1/2,−α1−α2−2​n)=(2α2+1)(2α2+3)⋯(2α2+2n−1)(2​n−1)!!​n!​Wn​((i​k)2,12,0,α1+12,−α1−α2−2​n)p_{2n}(-ik;\alpha_{1}+1/2,-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}-2n,\alpha_{1}+1/2,-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}-2n)=\\ \frac{(2\alpha_{2}+1)(2\alpha_{2}+3)\cdots(2\alpha_{2}+2n-1)}{(2n-1)!!\;n!}W_{n}\left((ik)^{2};\;\frac{1}{2},0,\alpha_{1}+\frac{1}{2},-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}-2n\right)

This identity demonstrates that the Mellin transforms satisfy a symmetry on the line Re⁡(k)=0\mathrm{Re}(k)=0 (the polynomials are invariant under k→−kk\to-k). Furthermore, by the orthogonality property (C.2), we can deduce that the zeros all lie on the imaginary axis (this does not seem to be obvious from the Hahn polynomial representation).

We now study the orthogonal ensemble with nn even. In this case the analytic structure of the Mellin transform seems to be more complicated and remains somewhat mysterious to us. For this reason we restrict ourselves to the Gaussian case, though analogous results for Laguerre and Jacobi could easily be derived. We are able to prove an analytic continuation of Qkℝ​(2​n)Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(2n) to an entire function of kk as in the previous sections, but with a more complicated structure. We first consider the simplest case n=2n=2 where this structure already appears. Directly integrating |x|2​k|x|^{2k} against the density (3.1) with β=1\beta=1 and a Gaussian weight gives

(8.41) Qkℝ(2)=2k​Γ​(k+1/2)π+12∫0∞x2​kxerf(x/2)e−x2/4dx.Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(2)=\frac{2^{k}\Gamma(k+1/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{2k}x\,\mathrm{erf}(x/2)e^{-x^{2}/4}\,dx.

Clearly, the first term above has a similar structure to that already observed in the GSE and GUE. But the second term, which is a weighted Mellin transform of the error function, is different. It is analytic in the half-plane Re⁡(2​k)>−1\mathrm{Re}(2k)>-1 and standard properties of Mellin transforms show that it extends as to an analytic function in the entire complex plane except for simple poles when 2​k+1∈{−2,−4,−6,…}2k+1\in\{-2,-4,-6,\ldots\}. Since these simple poles are eliminated on dividing by Γ⁡(k+1/2)\Gamma(k+1/2), this gives an entire function of kk. In fact this analytic continuation can be given in terms of a hypergeometric function:

Qkℝ​(2)\displaystyle Q_{k}^{\mathbb{R}}(2) =22​k+3/2​F12​(1/2,k+3/23/2,−1)​Γ​(k+3/2)/π+2k​Γ​(k+1/2)π\displaystyle=2^{2k+3/2}{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}1/2,k+3/2\\ 3/2\end{matrix};-1\right)\Gamma(k+3/2)/\sqrt{\pi}+\frac{2^{k}\Gamma(k+1/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}
=(2​k−1)!!​((2​k+1)​Mk​(−1, 3/2,1/2)+1).\displaystyle=(2k-1)!!\;\left((2k+1)M_{k}(-1;\;3/2,1/2)+1\right).

This hypergeometric function reduces to a polynomial whenever kk is a positive integer. But its analytic continuation to k∈ℂk\in\mathbb{C} appears more complicated than in the previously considered cases. Indeed one has the asymptotics (see e.g. [72]):

2F1(1/2,k+3/23/2;−1)∼12πk,k→+∞,2F1(1/2,k+3/23/2;−1)∼−k2−3/2−k,k→−∞.\begin{split}&{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}1/2,k+3/2\\ 3/2\end{matrix};-1\right)\sim\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{k}},\qquad k\to+\infty,\\ &{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\begin{matrix}1/2,k+3/2\\ 3/2\end{matrix};-1\right)\sim-k2^{-3/2-k},\qquad k\to-\infty.\end{split}

For say n=4,6,8,…n=4,6,8,\ldots and so on, this structure persists and follows a similar pattern. As for the GSE, the results of [62] are again useful here, providing a general formula for the GOE moments:

(8.42) Qkℝ​(2​n)=Qkℂ​(2​n−1)−∑j=0n−1∑i=0n−j−1(ki)​(ki+j)​(n−i−j)(k+1/2)(n−j)(1/2)+Akℝ​(2​n).Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(2n)=Q^{\mathbb{C}}_{k}(2n-1)-\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\sum_{i=0}^{n-j-1}{k\choose i}{k\choose i+j}\frac{(n-i-j)_{(k+1/2)}}{(n-j)_{(1/2)}}+A^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(2n).

where

Akℝ(2n):=cn∫0∞x2​ke−x2/2H2​n−1(x)erf(x/2)dx.A^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(2n):=c_{n}\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{2k}e^{-x^{2}/2}H_{2n-1}(x)\mathrm{erf}(x/\sqrt{2})\,dx.

The first two terms in (8.42) have a simple analytic structure, similar to that found in the symplectic case. The term Akℝ​(2​n)A^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(2n) is the generalization to larger nn of the second term in (8.41).

Proposition 8.11.

For any positive integer nn, the ratio Qkℝ​(2​n)/Γ⁡(k+1/2)Q^{\mathbb{R}}_{k}(2n)/\Gamma(k+1/2) has an analytic continuation to an entire function of kk.

Proof.

It is clear that the first two terms in (8.42) yield a polynomial in kk after dividing by Γ⁡(k+1/2)\Gamma(k+1/2). The third term (8.3) is the Mellin transform of the function ϕn(x)=e−x2/2H2​n−1(x)erf(x/2)\phi_{n}(x)=e^{-x^{2}/2}H_{2n-1}(x)\mathrm{erf}(x/\sqrt{2}) which is analytic in the right-half plane Re⁡(2​k)>−3\mathrm{Re}(2k)>-3. To extend to the left-half plane Re⁡(2​k)≤−3\mathrm{Re}(2k)\leq-3 it suffices to notice that ϕn​(x)\phi_{n}(x) has an asymptotic expansion near x=0x=0 with respect to the sequence {x2​k}k≥1\{x^{2k}\}_{k\geq 1}. Therefore A2​kℝ​(2​n)A^{\mathbb{R}}_{2k}(2n) has an meromorphic continuation into the left-half plane except for simple poles when 2​k+1=−2,−4,−6,…2k+1=-2,-4,-6,\ldots. Precisely these poles are eliminated after dividing through by the factor Γ⁡(k+1/2)\Gamma(k+1/2). ∎

The purpose of this section is to prove Proposition 8.8 in the three classical ensembles. Appendix B Mellin transform

We summarise here some properties of the Mellin transform (and its extension). The Mellin transform of f⁡(x)f(x) is defined by the integral

(B.1) ℳ⁡[f⁡(x);s]=∫0∞f⁡(x)​xs−1​𝑑x,\mathcal{M}\left[f(x);s\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty}f(x)x^{s-1}dx,

when it exists. We set f∗​(s)=ℳ⁡[f⁡(x);s]f^{*}(s)=\mathcal{M}\left[f(x);s\right].

In general, the integral (B.1) converges and defines a holomorphic function f∗​(s)f^{*}(s) only in a vertical strip DD of the complex plane. It turns out that, in the frequently occurring case where f⁡(x)f(x) is of rapid decay at infinity and has an asymptotic expansion f⁡(x)∼∑j=0∞aj​xbjf(x)\sim\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{j}x^{b_{j}} as x→0+x\to 0^{+} (as in all instances in this paper), the Mellin transform f∗​(s)f^{*}(s) has a meromorphic continuation to the whole complex plane with simple poles of residue aja_{j} at s=−bjs=-b_{j}. For more details on meromorphic extensions of Mellin transforms see [76].

If the integral (B.1) converges in the strip DD, then the following relations hold:

(B.2) ℳ​[f(m)​(x);s]\displaystyle\mathcal{M}\left[f^{(m)}(x);s\right] =(−1)m​(s−m)m​f∗​(s−m)\displaystyle=(-1)^{m}(s-m)_{m}f^{*}(s-m) s−m\displaystyle s-m ∈D\displaystyle\in D
(B.3) ℳ⁡[xm​f​(x);s]\displaystyle\mathcal{M}\left[x^{m}f(x);s\right] =f∗​(s+m)\displaystyle=f^{*}(s+m) s+m\displaystyle s+m ∈D\displaystyle\in D
(B.4) ℳ⁡[xm​f(m)​(x);s]\displaystyle\mathcal{M}\left[x^{m}f^{(m)}(x);s\right] =(−1)m​(s)m​f∗​(s)\displaystyle=(-1)^{m}(s)_{m}f^{*}(s) s\displaystyle s ∈D.\displaystyle\in D.

Suppose that f⁡(s)f(s) and g⁡(s)g(s) have Mellin transforms f∗​(s)f^{*}(s) and g∗​(s)g^{*}(s), respectively, analytic in a vertical strip DD in the complex plane. Take any c∈Dc\in D. Then

(B.5) ℳ⁡[f⁡(x)​g​(x);s]=12​π​i​∫c−i​∞c+i​∞f∗​(s−u)​g∗​(u)​𝑑u.\mathcal{M}\left[f(x)g(x);s\right]=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}f^{*}(s-u)g^{*}(u)du.

whenever the Mellin transfom of (f​g)​(x)(fg)(x) exists.

Appendix C Hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials

We report a few basic properties of some families of hypergeometric OP’s.

C.1. Wilson

The Wilson polynomials are solutions of the discrete Sturm-Liouville problem [48, Section 9.1]

(C.1) B⁡(x)​y​(x+i)−[B⁡(x)+D⁡(x)]​y​(x)+D⁡(x)​y​(x−i)=n⁡(n+a+b+c+d−1)​y​(x),B(x)y(x+i)-\left[B(x)+D(x)\right]y(x)+D(x)y(x-i)=n(n+a+b+c+d-1)y(x),

where

y⁡(x)=Wn​(x2,a,b,c,d)y(x)=W_{n}(x^{2};a,b,c,d)

and

{B⁡(x)=(a−i​x)​(b−i​x)​(c−i​x)​(d−i​x)2​i​x​(2​i​x−1)D⁡(x)=(a+i​x)​(b+i​x)​(c+i​x)​(d+i​x)2​i​x​(2​i​x+1).\left\{\begin{array}[]{l@{\quad}cr}\displaystyle B(x)=\frac{(a-ix)(b-ix)(c-ix)(d-ix)}{2ix(2ix-1)}\\ \\ \displaystyle D(x)=\frac{(a+ix)(b+ix)(c+ix)(d+ix)}{2ix(2ix+1)}.\end{array}\right.

In this paper we have considered the less conventional situation when a,b,c,1−d>0a,b,c,1-d>0. For this range of the parameters, Neretin [67, Section 3.3] found the orthogonality relation

12​π​∫ℝ+|Γ⁡(a+i​x)​Γ​(b+i​x)​Γ​(c+i​x)Γ⁡(1−d+i​x)​Γ​(2​i​x)|2​Wm​(x2,a,b,c,d)​Wn​(x2,a,b,c,d)​d⁡x\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\left|\frac{\Gamma(a+ix)\Gamma(b+ix)\Gamma(c+ix)}{\Gamma(1-d+ix)\Gamma(2ix)}\right|^{2}W_{m}(x^{2};\;a,b,c,d)W_{n}(x^{2};\;a,b,c,d)\operatorname{d}x
=a+b+c+d−1a+b+c+d+2​n−1​(a+b)n​(a+c)n​(a+d)n​(b+c)n​(b+d)n​(c+d)n(a+b+c+d−1)n\displaystyle=\frac{a+b+c+d-1}{a+b+c+d+2n-1}\frac{(a+b)_{n}(a+c)_{n}(a+d)_{n}(b+c)_{n}(b+d)_{n}(c+d)_{n}}{(a+b+c+d-1)_{n}}
(C.2) ×Γ⁡(a+b)​Γ​(a+c)​Γ​(b+c)​Γ​(1−a−b−c−d)Γ⁡(1−a−d)​Γ​(1−b−d)​Γ​(1−c−d)​n!​δm​n,\displaystyle\small\times\frac{\Gamma(a+b)\Gamma(a+c)\Gamma(b+c)\Gamma(1-a-b-c-d)}{\Gamma(1-a-d)\Gamma(1-b-d)\Gamma(1-c-d)}n!\;\delta_{mn},

for n,m<1−a−b−c−dn,m<1-a-b-c-d.

C.2. Continuous dual Hahn

The continuous dual Hahn polynomials Sn​(x2,a,b,c)S_{n}(x^{2};a,b,c) can be found from the Wilson polynomials by dividing by (a+d)n(a+d)_{n} and letting d→∞d\to\infty. If aa, bb and cc are positive, then [48, Section 9.3]

12​π​∫ℝ+|Γ⁡(a+i​x)​Γ​(b+i​x)​Γ​(c+i​x)Γ⁡(2​i​x)|2​Sm​(x2,a,b,c)​Sn​(x2,a,b,c)​d⁡x\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\left|\frac{\Gamma(a+ix)\Gamma(b+ix)\Gamma(c+ix)}{\Gamma(2ix)}\right|^{2}S_{m}(x^{2};\;a,b,c)S_{n}(x^{2};\;a,b,c)\operatorname{d}x
(C.3) =Γ⁡(n+a+b)​Γ​(n+a+c)​Γ​(n+b+c)​n!​δm​n.\displaystyle=\Gamma(n+a+b)\Gamma(n+a+c)\Gamma(n+b+c)n!\;\delta_{mn}.

The continuous dual Hahn polynomials are solution of the discrete Sturm-Liouville problem

(C.4) B⁡(x)​y​(x+i)−[B⁡(x)+D⁡(x)]​y​(x)+D⁡(x)​y​(x−i)=n​y​(x),B(x)y(x+i)-\left[B(x)+D(x)\right]y(x)+D(x)y(x-i)=ny(x),

where

y⁡(x)=Sn​(x2,a,b,c)y(x)=S_{n}(x^{2};a,b,c)

and

{B⁡(x)=(a−i​x)​(b−i​x)​(c−i​x)2​i​x​(2​i​x−1)D⁡(x)=(a+i​x)​(b+i​x)​(c+i​x)2​i​x​(2​i​x+1).\left\{\begin{array}[]{l@{\quad}cr}\displaystyle B(x)=\frac{(a-ix)(b-ix)(c-ix)}{2ix(2ix-1)}\\ \\ \displaystyle D(x)=\frac{(a+ix)(b+ix)(c+ix)}{2ix(2ix+1)}.\end{array}\right.

C.3. Meixner-Pollaczek

The Meixner-Pollaczek polynomials satisfy the orthogonality relation [48, Section 9.7]

12​π​∫ℝe(2​ϕ−π)​x​|Γ⁡(λ+i​x)|2​Pm(λ)​(x,ϕ)​Pn(λ)​(x,ϕ)​d⁡x\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{(2\phi-\pi)x}|\Gamma(\lambda+ix)|^{2}P_{m}^{(\lambda)}(x;\phi)P_{n}^{(\lambda)}(x;\phi)\operatorname{d}x
(C.5) =Γ⁡(n+2​λ)(2​sin⁡ϕ)2​λ​n!δm​n,λ>0and0<ϕ<π,\displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda)}{(2\sin\phi)^{2\lambda}n!}\;\delta_{mn},\quad\lambda>0\quad\text{and}\quad 0<\phi<\pi,

and the Sturm-Liouville equation (set y⁡(x)=Pn(λ)​(x,ϕ)y(x)=P_{n}^{(\lambda)}(x;\phi)):

(C.6) ei​ϕ​(λ−i​x)​y​(x+i)+2​i​x​cos⁡ϕ​y​(x)−e−i​ϕ​(λ+i​x)​y​(x−i)=2​i​(n+λ)​sin⁡ϕ​y​(x).e^{i\phi}(\lambda-ix)y(x+i)+2ix\cos\phi\;y(x)-e^{-i\phi}(\lambda+ix)y(x-i)=2i(n+\lambda)\sin\phi\;y(x).

C.4. Meixner polynomials

The Meixner polynomials satisfy the orthogonality relation [48, Section 9.7]

(C.7) ∑x=0∞(β)xx!​cx​Mm​(x,β,c)​Mn​(x,β,c)=n!(β)n​cn​(1−c)β​δm​n,β>0 and 0<c<1.\displaystyle\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\beta)_{x}}{x!}c^{x}M_{m}(x;\;\beta,c)M_{n}(x;\;\beta,c)=\frac{n!}{(\beta)_{n}c^{n}(1-c)^{\beta}}\delta_{mn},\quad\text{$\beta>0$ and $0<c<1$}.
